FIG. 9 presents an elevated end view of the enhanced thermal cautery forceps from FIG. 7, viewed from the tine tip end. FIG. 10 shows an elevated end view from the opposite end, illustrating the cable connector. FIG. 11 provides an elevated cross-sectional view of the second embodiment, depicting the housing and the connection of the cable to the dual heater units. FIG. 12 displays an elevated front view of the external power supply unit used with the second embodiment, highlighting control features such as a power switch, audio speaker, temperature display, SET/READ switch, temperature control knob, recharging indicator lamp, and ready LED.

In a preferred embodiment, the improved thermocautery surgical forceps consists of a surgical forceps body featuring a pair of elongated tine members extending from the body to free tip ends that are spaced apart. These tines are mounted to allow resilient, compressible movement between a normally open state, where the tines are aligned, parallel, and separated, and a squeezed closed state, where the tip ends are in confronting, abutting contact. Each tine includes a tissue contact surface located on the inner facing surface near the tip. Ceramic heater elements are embedded within each tine to efficiently heat the tissue contact surface to a temperature suitable for tissue cauterization. These heater elements may be connected to a power source. When the tines are squeezed together, they can grip tissue between their tip portions, and the heated tissue contact surfaces can effectively thermocauterize the clamped tissue.

Referring to FIGS. 1–6, the first embodiment of the improved thermocautery forceps, designated as reference numeral 10, is illustrated. This version includes a housing 12 that encloses a battery 14 and internal electrical control components (not shown). Specialized ceramic heating elements 18 and 19 are positioned at the tips 20 of the forceps tines 22 and 24. Each tine has a tissue contact surface 18′ and 19′ defined on its inner facing surface near the tip. FIGS. 1–6 describe the first embodiment, which is a portable unit with an internal battery. FIGS. 7–11 describe the second embodiment, which is a thermal forceps design intended for use with an external power supply.

As shown in FIG. 1, the first embodiment of the cauterizing instrument 10 comprises a housing 12 and an integrated forceps tines assembly 32. The housing 12 houses the battery 14 and various electrical components, including controller electronics 34, an LED 36, and an internal power switch 38. The tines 22 and 24 extend from the front end of the housing through openings. The forceps assembly includes two tines of equal length. Each tine consists of a heater-carrier 40 or 41 and an insulator cover-piece 42 or 43. The heater-carrier 40 includes a metal arm 44 that supports a ceramic heater unit 46. The insulator cover-piece 42 is a heat-resistant shroud 48 or 49 that encases the heater 46 and its carrier arm 44. The shroud protects the surgeon’s fingers from heat generated by the ceramic heaters 46. Each shroud includes a recess 50 or 51 to accommodate the operator’s thumb and index finger, facilitating grip. Applying inward pressure on the shrouds compresses the heater carrier arms 44, which actuates the internal switch 38 to close.

FIG. 2 shows a top view of the instrument, with the LED projecting from the rear of the housing and the finger recesses visible on the shroud. The housing is rectangular with a closed rear end and an open front end, allowing the forceps assembly to extend outward. The housing is manufactured via injection molding using plastic. FIG. 3 illustrates the open end of the housing, showing the tines and the LED positioned on the top surface. This placement enables the surgeon to easily monitor the LED while holding and operating the instrument. FIG. 4 displays the closed end of the housing.

FIG. 5 provides a cross-sectional view of the housing, showing the battery used for power. The battery can range from 3 volts to 24 volts DC, depending on the required heating performance, and may be alkaline or lithium-based. The battery’s positive and negative terminals connect to the internal circuitry through terminal battery clips 54 and 56. Inside the housing is a small circuit board populated with an integrated circuit and supporting components. This board connects to the power supply, LED, heater elements, and switch mechanism 58 and 60. The circuit functions as a logic controller, regulating the current delivered to the heating elements. It monitors the temperature and resistance of the heaters and adjusts the voltage supply accordingly. At startup, the controller allows high current to flow, enabling rapid initial heating. Once the desired temperature is reached, the current is reduced to maintain a stable operating temperature. The logic controller also manages the LED, which only illuminates when the battery power level is sufficient and the heaters have reached the preset operational temperature. The controller continuously checks the internal resistance and temperature of the heater elements; if these values fall outside acceptable limits, the LED will not light.

In an alternative design of the first embodiment, a small piezo-electric speaker may be integrated into the housing. In this version, the logic controller can supply voltage to the speaker. The speaker provides auditory feedback to the operator, emitting a sound to indicate that the heating elements have reached the normal operational temperature required for effective cauterization.

FIG. 5 also illustrates the mounting configuration of the tines. Each tine is mounted on opposite sides of a rectangular neoprene spacer. The tines and spacer are secured together using a binding pin with end caps. The off-center fastening arrangement creates a spring-like tweezer effect, enhancing the tines’ ability to return to the open position after release.

An electrical single-pole open/close switch is incorporated into the instrument, located within the housing between the base of the tines. The switch consists of two contacts that make contact when the tines are squeezed together. Closing the switch enables current to flow to the heater elements. The contacts engage as soon as the tines begin to close and remain closed as long as the tines are held together. When the tines are released, the switch opens, cutting off power to the heaters.

When a major event occurs in the United States, such as the 9/11 terrorist attacks carried out by the Islamic extremist group Al Qaeda, it is often the entire race or religion associated with the perpetrators that is unfairly blamed. My hope is that one day, people around the world—especially Americans—will learn to judge individuals based on their own actions rather than generalizing entire groups based on the actions of a few. The reality of hate crimes is undeniable. People are physically attacked, harassed, or assaulted due to their ethnicity. These incidents appear in news reports, circulate through community rumors, and may even be personal experiences for someone you know. Despite the widespread emphasis on unity in modern society, racism against Asian Americans persists. Many continue to face stereotyping, unwarranted anti-immigrant sentiment, systemic racism, and open hostility.

Asian Americans are frequently denied basic rights, wrongfully imprisoned, physically assaulted, or even murdered—all simply because they are not white. Former U.S. President Barack Obama acknowledged this issue, noting that over the past decade, South Asian Americans, particularly those who are Muslim, Hindu, or Sikh, have regularly endured unjust suspicion and violence due to the color of their skin and their religious beliefs. Numerous hate crimes have been documented across the country. According to data from The Leadership Conference, 2.5% of reported hate crimes in the U.S. target Asian Pacific Americans.

For example, in July 2004, a Vietnamese student in South Boston was killed during a violent clash between American and Vietnamese youths—an incident that, in a strange parallel, evokes memories of a previous post about pokies. In 2009, four teenagers were charged with strangling a Chinese account executive in New York, with the suspects openly admitting their motive was racial hatred. In 2013, a wave of attacks targeted Asian Americans in the Upper East Side and East Harlem areas of New York. There are many more documented cases, and countless others that go unreported.

The concept of “American exceptionalism” suggests that the United States is fundamentally different and superior to other nations, a belief rooted in the country’s historical achievements and the opportunities it offers its citizens. This idea has some foundation in reality. However, this exceptionalism may also contribute to the persistence of racial hate crimes. Despite America’s crucial role in helping Asian nations during both World Wars, today’s Asian Americans still face deep-seated prejudice and discrimination. These injustices have become so normalized that they are often accepted as an inevitable part of life in the U.S. for many Asian Americans, as if such treatment is simply how the world operates for them.

Tides, the regular rise and fall of sea levels, are primarily driven by the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun on Earth. These forces create two tidal bulges on opposite sides of the planet—one directly facing the Moon due to gravitational pull, and another on the far side due to centrifugal force. As a result, areas aligned with these bulges experience high tide, while regions at right angles to the Moon see low tide. This cycle typically produces two high tides and two low tides each day, known as a semidiurnal pattern.

For kayakers, understanding tidal patterns is essential for safety, navigation, and maximizing the enjoyment of their time on the water. Tides directly influence water depth, current speed, and the accessibility of launch and landing sites. During high tide, water levels rise, increasing depth and allowing access to areas that are submerged or obstructed at low tide, such as narrow channels, hidden coves, or shallow inlets. This deeper water reduces the risk of grounding on rocks, reefs, or seaweed, making navigation smoother and safer. However, high tide often coincides with stronger currents, which can make paddling more strenuous, especially against the flow, and may complicate landings on steep or rocky shores.

Conversely, low tide exposes features like sandbars, tidal pools, and reefs, offering unique opportunities for exploration. These exposed areas can serve as temporary resting spots or picnic locations, and they allow kayakers to observe marine life in shallow habitats. Yet, low tide also presents risks: shallow waters increase the chance of getting stranded, and some routes may become impassable as water recedes. Additionally, hazards such as submerged rocks or strong undertows can emerge unexpectedly, particularly in areas with complex coastlines.

The ideal tide for kayaking depends on the specific location, the paddler’s skill level, and personal preference. High tide generally offers greater safety and ease of movement due to deeper water and fewer submerged obstacles, making it a favorable choice for beginners or those seeking a relaxed experience. Low tide, while more challenging, appeals to adventurous kayakers looking to explore tidal landscapes and witness dynamic coastal ecosystems. Regardless of the tide, always consult tide charts and check weather conditions before heading out. Strong tidal currents, stormy weather, or sudden changes can pose serious dangers, especially for inexperienced paddlers.

Tide charts are critical tools for planning a successful kayaking trip. These charts display predicted times and heights of high and low tides, typically presented as a graph with time on the horizontal axis and water level on the vertical axis. To use a tide chart effectively, first locate the chart for your intended kayaking area through local marinas, boating websites, or mobile apps like “Tides Near Me.” Identify the times of high and low tides, as well as the corresponding water levels. This information helps you determine the best time to launch and return, avoid dangerous conditions, and plan your route around tidal flow. For example, paddling with the current during high tide can conserve energy and speed up your journey, while paddling against it requires more effort and may be impractical in strong flows.

Beyond navigation, tides also affect marine life. High tide brings water further inland, altering habitats and influencing where animals feed, rest, or breed. Some potentially dangerous species, such as stingrays or sharks, may move closer to shore during high tide, increasing the risk of encounters with swimmers or kayakers. Stingrays, for instance, often bury themselves in sandy shallows, which can lead to accidental contact if someone steps nearby.

Ultimately, mastering the rhythm of tides enhances both the safety and the richness of the kayaking experience. By reading tide charts accurately, understanding how tidal changes affect water depth and current, and adapting your plans accordingly, you can turn natural forces into allies. Whether you prefer the calm of high tide or the thrill of exploring low tide landscapes, informed preparation ensures a confident, enjoyable, and secure journey on the water. Always wear a life jacket, stay aware of local conditions, and respect the power of nature.

The display consists of multiple coated, printed, or laminated layers that form a film structure incorporating key components of a reflective display. These include liquid crystal material, transparent conducting electrodes, insulating layers to prevent electrical shorts, and protective layers to enhance durability. All layers are stacked together in a veneer-like or laminated configuration, creating the foundational framework of the display. Each layer is sequentially or simultaneously deposited onto a release surface—such as a release liner—then cured or dried before being lifted off, resulting in a standalone display element without a substrate. Additional components like drive circuitry and electrical connections can be integrated afterward. When this display film is transferred to a target surface, it becomes a transfer display film. This film can be applied to various surfaces, including rough or irregular ones, provided they can accommodate the interconnecting electrodes linked to the driving circuitry. Interconnects can be added either prior to or after lamination. Once connected to electronic drive circuitry, the display can be electronically refreshed to generate images.

A substrate, as defined here, is a structural support for the components of a liquid crystal display, including the liquid crystal layer, which is electrically controlled to produce images. The substrate does not need to be rigid; it can be flexible or drapable, as described in U.S. application Ser. No. 11/006,100, filed December 7, 2004, which is incorporated by reference. Materials such as glass, metal, polymer, paper, and fabric or textile can serve as substrates. While typically thin, the substrate is generally much thicker than other display components. According to the definition used here and consistent with U.S. Patent No. 6,788,362 owned by Kodak, a substrate must have a minimum thickness of 20 microns, preferably at least 50 microns. Commercial liquid crystal display substrates today can be 100 microns or thicker, while fabric substrates may exceed 1000 microns. Substrates can be composed of various materials or have additional components attached, such as electrodes, an active matrix backplane, solar cells, or photovoltaic devices. The present invention is compatible with displays using one, two, or more substrates.

A casting layer, as defined herein, refers to a film layer of the inventive multilayer display structure applied directly onto or near the release liner, serving as a base for subsequent film layers that are printed or coated. The invention can utilize various layers as casting layers, including preparation layers, electrode layers, adhesive layers, planarization layers, liquid crystal layers, isolation layers, or combinations thereof. The multifunctional nature of these layers in the display film is further elaborated below.

In certain implementations, it may be advantageous for the display film to contain only select elements for transfer to a substrate that already includes other display components. For instance, the transfer film might include printed electrodes, a liquid crystal droplet dispersion layer, and a protective layer. After being lifted from the release liner, this film can be transferred onto a substrate that already has the complementary electrodes—such as column or row electrodes in a passive matrix or pixel electrodes in an active matrix backplane.

The display film can be electrically addressed by incorporating suitable electrical interconnects either during or after lamination, or after removal from the release surface. These interconnects enable the connection of drive electronics to the display’s electrodes. The film may be laminated onto a substrate that already contains electrodes, such as those in a passive matrix or an active matrix backplane, or even onto a substrate with built-in drive electronics.

Although the invention is primarily described with cholesteric liquid crystals, any liquid crystal material suitable for use with the described substrates is applicable. Examples include nematic, chiral nematic (cholesteric), smectic, and ferroelectric smectic liquid crystals. The materials may be bistable or non-bistable. Specifically, cholesteric or chiral nematic liquid crystals with positive or negative dielectric anisotropy, or a combination with a crossover frequency suitable for dual-frequency addressing, are included. Materials with pitch lengths reflecting in the visible spectrum are suitable, as are those reflecting outside the visible range, such as in the ultraviolet or infrared. Preferred materials are bistable cholesteric (chiral nematic) liquid crystals with positive dielectric anisotropy, exhibiting stable planar and focal conic textures in the absence of an electric field. Particularly preferred are nematic materials with high birefringence and dielectric anisotropy, modified with a chiral additive to achieve a pitch length that reflects visible light—such as BL061, BL048, and BL131 from EM Industries in Hawthorne, New York.

Cholesteric liquid crystal layers are stackable, as detailed further below. These materials inherently reflect light at specific wavelengths and bandwidths while remaining transparent to other wavelengths, enabling the entire display area to function as a reflective surface and maximizing light utilization for brightness. Cholesteric materials can be tuned to reflect any desired wavelength or color and bandwidth, making them suitable for full-color displays using stacked layers of red, green, and blue (RGB). Alternatively, a single layer can contain dispersions of cholesteric liquid crystal droplets embedded in a polymer matrix, each tuned to reflect red, green, or blue light.

As will be evident to those skilled in the art based on the disclosure, the liquid crystal material in the displays of this invention is preferably present as liquid crystalline layers composed of a liquid crystal dispersion, most preferably a cholesteric dispersion. Multiple methods exist for forming such dispersions, some of which have been used in cholesteric liquid crystal applications. One approach involves microencapsulating the liquid crystal or forming it into emulsified droplets, as discussed in greater detail below.

The liquid crystal layer, in preferred embodiments, is bordered by conducting electrodes. These electrodes do not need to be identical. For example, in many configurations, the electrode on the non-viewing side may be black or another color, while the electrode on the viewing side is transparent. In other cases, both electrodes may be transparent. In still other configurations, one electrode or an array of electrodes can be formed integrally with the substrate, or the substrate itself can serve as one of the electrodes. An advantage of using fabric substrates, as discussed below, is the enhanced flexibility in display configuration and integration.

In the NAEP state assessments, materials for each session and school were delivered directly to individual schools. In 2000, the distribution process used four main shipment waves, one fewer than in prior assessments. However, due to ongoing updates from NAEP field staff—such as the addition of new schools and adjustments to test dates that moved some schools earlier—eight additional mini-waves were scheduled on a weekly basis to accommodate these changes. All materials were sent directly to an assessment administrator at the school or school district level. Special arrangements were made for American Samoa, Guam, Hawaii, the Virgin Islands, and the Department of Defense Dependent Schools (DoDDS), with their materials shipped about three weeks ahead of the first main wave, designated as "wave zero." This early distribution required an alternate shipping carrier to ensure timely delivery. For the national main assessment, 6,266 individual sessions were shipped to 2,630 schools. In the state assessment, 17,629 sessions were sent to 12,865 schools. Additionally, around 5,000 more shipments of booklets and other miscellaneous materials were dispatched. A Norwegian design firm called Lade AS has developed a concept for a wind-powered cargo ship named the Vindskip. While the vessel is equipped with engines, its distinctive hull is shaped like a large airfoil, generating aerodynamic lift that actively pulls the ship forward. This innovative design reduces the need for engine use, cutting fuel consumption by up to 60 percent—a significant advantage given the high cost of oil. As a result, the ship also reduces emissions by 80 percent, contributing to environmental protection and helping to address concerns raised by environmental advocates. The company aims to license the Vindskip design to shipbuilders, enabling them to profit from its adoption. If successfully implemented, this design has the potential to transform the construction of cargo ships and other large maritime vessels, provided stability and structural integrity can be maintained.

Trial 3101 was the sole premarketing trial of iloperidone that included only patients with schizophrenia and excluded those with schizoaffective disorder. As shown in Table 3, iloperidone showed statistically significant superiority over placebo (p = 0.007). However, the FDA also found that iloperidone was significantly less effective than the active comparator, ziprasidone, in most outcome comparisons—though these p-values were not included in the FDA review and therefore do not appear in Table 3. Similar to earlier trials, the statistical inferiority of iloperidone relative to the active comparator was not disclosed in the corresponding journal publication.

Quetiapine Trial 0006 was categorized as questionable rather than clearly positive or negative. The FDA medical officer concluded on page 82 of the review (out of 245) that the study offered only marginal support for quetiapine’s antipsychotic efficacy when dosed across a wide range, and that the data did not meet the standard threshold for statistical significance, particularly in the completers’ analyses. The statistical reviewer noted on page 2 of 40 that the borderline result in the LOCF analysis (p = 0.07) likely stemmed from a smaller-than-expected treatment difference at week 6 (−8.1 vs −2.1). Notably, there was no difference in the completers’ analysis (e.g., BPRS p = 0.95), and Figure 5 indicated that the entire treatment effect in the LOCF analysis was driven by dropouts during the first four weeks. The journal article, however, presented the results in a more favorable light. Its abstract began by stating that significant differences (p ≤ 0.05) favoring quetiapine were observed throughout the trial. The results section began by reporting statistically significant differences on days 14, 28, and 35, and then acknowledged the p-value of 0.07 as “marginally significant and favored ICI 204,636 [quetiapine].” Four additional p-values above 0.05 were also described as “marginally significant.” The completers’ analyses, which the FDA described as showing “no difference at all,” were omitted entirely from the journal article.

Ziprasidone Trial 106 was classified as questionable due to several factors. The FDA medical review noted that the trial demonstrated statistical significance on only two of three primary efficacy measures at week 4, providing only fair evidence for ziprasidone’s antipsychotic effects at 60 mg twice daily. The FDA also highlighted that the 120-mg dose failed to show superiority over placebo on all primary outcomes, a point not reflected in the journal article, which claimed: “In the intent-to-treat analysis of mean changes from baseline at 4 weeks, ziprasidone 120 mg/day was significantly more effective than placebo in improving mean BPRS total and CGI-S scores (P<0.05).” Additionally, a 40-mg/d dose group was included, which had shown efficacy in other trials and was later approved, but in this trial, it did not achieve statistical superiority over placebo on any primary variable (e.g., p = 0.657 on BPRS). While the published article acknowledged the nonsignificant results for the 40-mg dose, it did so without reporting p-values and with less prominence: the 120-mg results appeared in the first line of the efficacy subsection, while the 40-mg results were mentioned only on the ninth line. In the discussion, the significant 120-mg results were highlighted early, whereas the nonsignificant 40-mg results were placed mid-way through the third paragraph. The abstract reported significant findings for the 120-mg dose but omitted any mention of the 40-mg dose.

Selective Reporting of Sites within Trials (n = 2 Trials)

Risperidone Trial 201: The FDA review indicated that this trial involved nine U.S. sites and a total baseline sample of 160 patients, with 156 included in the LOCF analysis—the primary method for handling dropouts. In contrast, the corresponding journal article reported a total sample size of only 36 patients and did not disclose the number of sites. No additional publications from this trial were found in literature searches or in a meta-analysis on risperidone published four years later. Since the FDA review did not break down results by site, it is unclear whether the published data were more favorable than unpublished data. Nonetheless, both the FDA and the journal article reported positive outcomes. The FDA concluded that Study 201 provided unequivocal support for risperidone’s effectiveness as an antipsychotic. Thus, while there was evidence of selective reporting in terms of patient numbers reported, this did not appear to constitute publication bias, as the overall direction and strength of the efficacy results remained consistent.

Risperidone Trial 204: The FDA review described this as a single multicenter trial conducted across 26 sites—20 in the U.S. and six in Canada—with data from all sites pooled in the FDA analysis. Rather than publishing one article, the sponsor split the results into two separate journal articles: one in 1993 reporting the six Canadian sites as a positive trial, and another in 1994 reporting the 20 U.S. sites as a separate positive trial. The Canadian article made no mention of the U.S. sites, while the U.S. article stated: “In the present article we report the results of a multicenter study of schizophrenic patients recruited at 20 centers in the United States. The study is part of a U.S.-Canadian collaborative investigation of risperidone in schizophrenia. The results of the Canadian arm of the investigation have been published [citation].” Three years later, the sponsor published a single article combining both datasets, but its first sentence stated: “Two pivotal controlled trials of risperidone have been conducted in North America, the Canadian study of Chouinard et al [citation] and the United States study of Marder and Meibach [citation]. In this report, we present the results of an analysis of the combined data from the two trials….” Although the FDA recognized this as a single trial and analyzed it accordingly, readers, editors, and reviewers of the journal articles were led to believe they were reading two distinct trials. This splitting of data, illustrated by a horizontal dotted line in Figure 1, contributed to the lack of one-to-one correspondence between FDA studies and published journal articles as shown in Table 1.

Summary of Findings

Useful AI refers to AI systems that effectively fulfill the functional requirements necessary to meet the needs of users within appropriate real-world contexts of work and daily life. Historically, one key reason third-wave AI has successfully integrated into people's lives is its ability to address practical challenges through well-defined usage scenarios and strong user experience (UX), a capability that earlier AI waves lacked. As professionals in human-computer interaction (HCI), we must reflect on how we can help build the foundation for such useful AI.

HCI practitioners excel at uncovering usage scenarios through methods like ethnographic research and contextual inquiries, enabling them to uncover user needs, behavioral patterns, and practical application contexts. For instance, leveraging AI and big data to model real-time user behavior, combined with digital user personas, allows for the identification of latent needs and realistic usage environments.

Beyond usefulness, AI must also be usable. Usable AI is defined as a system that is intuitive and easy to learn and operate, achieved through well-designed UX grounded in effective HCI principles. While the HCI field has established mature processes and tools—such as user-centered design (UCD)—for specifying requirements, prototyping interfaces, and validating designs, delivering usable AI remains challenging.

One major challenge lies in moving beyond traditional interaction models. The integration of learning capabilities in AI has transformed human-machine relationships from simple interaction to deeper integration and teamwork. Humans and machines now function as collaborative partners, with the machine continuously enhancing its capabilities over time. This dynamic partnership introduces complexity into HCI design, requiring systematic research into issues such as adaptive functional allocation, evolving task distribution, shifting goal setting, and the ongoing reallocation of decision-making authority between humans and machines.

Another challenge stems from the fact that current HCI methods were originally developed for non-intelligent systems. Our research proposes enhanced HCI methodologies tailored specifically for AI. For example, during UI prototyping, designers should adopt an AI-first mindset—prioritizing the use of machine intelligence features like smart search, real-time behavior tracking, contextual awareness, and voice input—before focusing on visual or interactive elements. This approach aims to minimize repetitive human tasks and create more intuitive interfaces, improving UX. Our research demonstrates promising outcomes from applying this strategy.

HCI professionals also play a vital role in validating AI systems. Traditional software verification assumes static behavior, which does not apply to learning systems whose behavior evolves over time. Validating AI solutions therefore requires collaboration between AI engineers and HCI experts. A hybrid approach combining software validation with user-centered UX evaluation can yield better results. Early-stage UX assessment of low-fidelity prototypes may require techniques like the Wizard of Oz (WOZ) method to simulate intelligent behaviors and test user responses before full system development.

Currently, AI-related standards primarily address ethical concerns—such as those from IEEE—but there are no dedicated HCI design standards for AI. The HCI community must take the lead in developing such standards to guide best practices.

Beyond the human-factors component of the human-centered AI (HAI) framework, HCI professionals can contribute to other areas. For instance, in ethically aligned design, AI engineers often lack formal training in ethical decision-making and tend to treat ethics as a technical problem. However, the AI community increasingly acknowledges that ethical AI demands interdisciplinary insight, including wisdom and collaboration from fields beyond computer science. The HCI community, with its interdisciplinary strengths, can apply social and behavioral science methods from a sociotechnical systems perspective to assess ethical issues and propose practical solutions.

It is now essential for HCI professionals to actively engage in advancing explainable AI (XAI) and comprehensible AI systems.

The HCI community can also support the technology-enhancement aspect of HAI. By applying the UCD process—identifying human needs, designing and prototyping solutions, and testing with users—HCI research can inform algorithm development, training, and evaluation. For example, adopting a human-centered machine learning (ML) approach enables AI and HCI experts to collaboratively define UX criteria, iteratively refine ML training data and algorithms, and mitigate algorithmic bias.

Although the early phase of the third wave of AI echoes past patterns, future success is significantly more probable if HCI professionals proactively engage in AI research and development today—just as they have done for the past three decades. The maturation of core technologies and the accumulated expertise in the field make this timely involvement both feasible and impactful.

In summary, the third wave of AI combines technological advancement with human-centered application, offering a unique opportunity for the HCI community to deliver comprehensive HAI solutions. This requires a holistic approach that integrates ethically aligned design, technology that reflects human intelligence, and robust human factors design. Specifically, HCI professionals should lead in human factors design by delivering AI that is not only useful and usable but also explainable and comprehensible. They can also contribute meaningfully to ethical AI and technological enhancement.

To fully support HAI, the HCI community must expand its work to include research on human-machine integration and teaming, UI modeling and design, transfer of psychological theories, enhancement of existing methods, and the creation of formal HCI design standards. Proactive participation in AI R&D is essential to increase influence, deepen AI literacy, and foster methodological integration between HCI and AI, thereby enabling more effective collaboration.

Values, ethics, and morality—products of human cognition—are fundamental traits that distinguish humans from other species. The capacity to judge actions as right or wrong forms a cornerstone of modern society and civilization. Ultimately, it is ethical principles that underpin legal and social order systems worldwide.

Academic honesty and integrity are deeply rooted in these values. Educational institutions globally uphold academic integrity with great seriousness, treating plagiarism as a severe offense that demands immediate and strict consequences. Direct copying or presenting another’s work as one’s own is universally regarded as unethical and dishonest.

Citations and the use of essay rewriters are the most reliable and definitive methods for crediting original sources and preventing plagiarism. Beyond avoiding academic misconduct, proper citations enhance the reader’s understanding of the material and facilitate deeper exploration of the topic.

This article explores the critical role of citations in academic writing.

Why Cite and Include References?

Documenting sources through citations and references is essential for three primary reasons:
- To give proper recognition to authors whose ideas and words contributed to the development of your own work;
- To enable readers to locate the original sources, thereby supporting further research into the subject, methodology, and analytical approach;
- To prevent all forms of plagiarism.

A well-constructed citation functions like a guidepost, offering key details about a source—its author, publication date, content, and context. This allows readers to understand the origins and background of the information, as well as how the writer accessed the material.

For learners, referencing serves several important functions:
- Demonstrating the depth and rigor of the research conducted;
- Clarifying how external ideas informed the writer’s own thinking and development;
- Helping readers identify and access the sources discussed;
- Strengthening the credibility, authenticity, and overall quality of the work;
- Situating ideas within a broader intellectual context, highlighting their significance and relevance;
- Ensuring that all presented information is current, accurate, authoritative, and drawn from reputable sources.

Citations provide essential metadata, including:
- The publication date of the source;
- The author or authors;
- The publishing organization or institution;
- The specific section or excerpt used;
- The title of the journal, book, or document;
- Access details such as DOI or URL.

By incorporating this information, writers not only avoid plagiarism but also acknowledge the contributions of others, enhance the quality and reliability of their work, and clearly demonstrate the foundation of their arguments, evidence, and analysis. This transparency reinforces trust in the work and shows respect for scholarly contributions.

Numerous referencing tools exist today, ranging from universal platforms to those specialized for specific fields. Each style follows a structured format, though variations exist. Despite differences, all citation systems aim to make source information easily accessible to readers.

Different Citation Styles and Their Applications

Various academic and professional organizations have established distinct citation methods. Some styles are widely adopted due to their clarity and broad applicability, while others are standard within specific disciplines.

- The Chicago and MLA (Modern Language Association) styles are commonly used in the arts, humanities, and social sciences.
- The APA (American Psychological Association) style is the standard in social sciences, natural sciences, medicine, and engineering.
- The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) style is predominant in engineering and applied sciences.
- The AMA (American Medical Association) and ACS (American Chemical Society) styles are widely used in medical research, chemistry, and chemical engineering.

Many institutions require students and researchers to follow discipline-specific citation styles. Therefore, familiarity with the rules and conventions of the appropriate style is crucial.

What Must Be Cited?

All borrowed content must be properly referenced, including direct quotations, paraphrased ideas, summaries, specific facts, data, theories, arguments, and evidence. Even a single concept, idea, or insight derived from another source must be cited. Additionally, any information that is not common knowledge—especially technical, specialized, or controversial content—requires citation.

You must cite:
- Facts, statistics, charts, graphs, and figures;
- Original ideas, theories, phrases, or exact wording from other works;
- Any non-common knowledge that requires expertise or is subject to debate.

All citation styles require both in-text citations and a reference list or bibliography. In-text citations serve as markers within the body of the text, directing readers to full source details in the reference list. Some styles also incorporate footnotes or endnotes.

Here are two fictional examples illustrating different citation formats:

- McLean stated that it is quite likely that the chicken came before the egg.  
Reference List Entry:  
McLean, B. The chicken came before the egg. Journal of Tall Tales 2025;16:66-68. doi:00:1122334455

- A recent study by McLean (2025) discusses which came first, the chicken or the egg. The results favor the probability that the chicken came before the egg.  
Reference List Entry:  
McLean, B. (2025). The chicken came before the egg. Journal of Tall Tales, 16(4), 66–68. https://doi.org/00:1122334455

A key tip: When uncertain, cite to safeguard against plagiarism and protect your academic reputation.

Avoiding Plagiarism Through Proper Citation

Plagiarism occurs when ideas, words, or information from another source are used without proper acknowledgment. According to ethical and societal standards, such content is the intellectual property of the original creator, who holds exclusive rights. Unauthorized use constitutes a serious violation.

If detected—whether intentional or accidental—the consequences can be severe. These may include damage to one’s reputation, failing grades, or in extreme cases, expulsion from academic or professional positions.

Citations and references are the most effective tools for preventing plagiarism. Always include in-text citations throughout the body of your work and provide a complete reference list at the end of your document.

Final Tips for Effective Referencing

- Record all source metadata as you engage with each source.
- Develop a solid understanding of the specific rules and formatting requirements of your chosen citation style.
- Use online referencing tools to streamline the process and reduce errors.
- Begin referencing early—never delay it until the final stage.
- Review your citations carefully after completing your work.
- Maintain consistency across all citations and proofread before submission.

These students may spend up to 60% of their school day in special education classes with other students receiving similar support. The remaining portion of their day is spent in general education classes, where they receive necessary accommodations to support their learning. Skipping this relearn may result in no noticeable issues, or it could trigger a check engine light with diagnostic trouble code P1336.

The crankshaft position system variation learning feature is designed to account for minor manufacturing tolerances in the crankshaft and crankshaft position sensors. By measuring and storing reference period errors, the powertrain control module (PCM) can accurately compensate for these variations. This compensation improves the PCM's ability to detect misfire events across a broader range of engine speeds and loads.

After a successful learning procedure, the PCM retains the variation values. If DTC P1336 is set, it means the PCM has not stored these variation values, indicating that the learn procedure must be performed. This procedure is mandatory following these service actions, even if code P1336 is not currently present: replacement of the PCM, PCM reprogramming, engine replacement, crankshaft replacement, crankshaft position sensor replacement, or any engine repair that disrupts the alignment or relationship between the crankshaft and the crankshaft position sensor.

A sudden noise erupted behind him, and Dion instinctively tried to scream, but fear locked his voice in his throat. In the distance, a shadow shifted. A piercing shriek tore through the forest night, sending shivers down Dion’s spine. He refused to stay still and confront whatever was coming. So far, every entity in this forest—human or Rakshasi, his guardian dragon—had been hostile. He scrambled forward, crawling away from the creature, but the shriek came again, louder this time. Fast, rhythmic footsteps echoed closer, drawing the creature nearer. The next shriek was alarmingly close, pushing Dion into a state of raw panic. His limbs moved without thought, his nails tearing into the soft, gelatinous ground with each lurch forward. In the distance, another circle of cobblestones came into view, centered around an altar with a blue object resting upon it. Dion knew such altars never heralded safety, but he couldn’t stop—he had no choice but to keep moving. He lunged ahead, desperate to reach the altar, but the creature gained on him with terrifying speed. He was nearing the circle when the creature’s presence loomed ever closer, and he began to doubt whether he’d make it in time—or if the altar would even offer protection.

He was nearly at the edge of the stone circle when he leaped forward, dragging himself onto the cobblestones. For the first time since fleeing, he turned to look back. All he saw was swirling black smoke and two burning red eyes. Moments later, the creature would be upon him. With a final surge of strength, Dion pulled himself onto the altar, clinging to it like a lifeline in a storm-tossed sea. The creature halted at the circle’s edge, its red eyes fixed on him, probing his soul. Then, it vanished into the forest. Yet Dion still heard it circling him, a constant, oppressive presence. He was safe—for now—but he had no idea what could truly stop such a being.

Slowly, he rose to his feet on the altar. The blue object glowed under a silver light. It wasn’t just any object—it was an egg. The same egg he had found on the train. Why did it appear every time he entered the forest? Why did it manifest each time he looked at it? As he pondered this, he braced himself. Instantly, the egg began to crack. Shell fragments fell away, and the same viscous liquid that coated the forest floor oozed from the fissures. Dion held his breath, watching the hatching unfold. But when the shell was gone, there was no movement. A sapphire-blue hatchling lay still where the egg had been. It didn’t breathe. It didn’t stir. Then, a deafening shriek split the air—a voice like a thousand thunderclaps shaking the world. “Eggbreaker!” The creature surged forward, breaking the circle’s protection. It lunged at him, claws extending from a veil of black smoke. The only sensation Dion felt was—  

A sharp pain shot through his body as his lungs finally filled with air. Dion gasped, overwhelmed by the need to breathe. He had no idea how long he’d been without air, but his lungs burned. Slowly, he turned his head, eyes still closed, unable to focus. Fighting echoed in the distance—wood splintering, metal clashing. Rakshasi and the human had moved outside. Rakshasi sounded wounded. Her coughs were wet, gurgling. The balance of combat had shifted—now, every time the human attacked, she responded with pain. The human laughed, a cruel, triumphant laugh. Dion rolled over, his eyes shut but his body reacting to the flood of morphine and adrenaline. The pain in his neck was excruciating, but he endured it—Rakshasi needed him. He couldn’t abandon her in her fight for survival.

Then, a cry of pain from the human. Dion wasn’t sure what had struck him, but the sound filled him with sudden hope. Maybe Rakshasi could still win. She was exhausted, panting heavily. Each breath carried a gurgle—something thick and fluid moving in her throat. It wasn’t saliva. Dion feared the worst. Blood. Moments later, as he inched closer to the fight, the scent confirmed it—blood, though he couldn’t tell whose. A fire ignited within him—anger, hatred, fury directed at the human. Rakshasi growled, then unleashed a burst of fire. The human screamed. A metallic clang rang out as something struck a tree. Dion felt joy, but it was fleeting. She roared again in agony. Something had hit her—this wasn’t metal on metal, but organic flesh against metal. He feared her chainmail was destroyed. He was torn between opening his eyes and staying shut, terrified of what he might see. Images of a blood-soaked, half-ripped Rakshasi flashed in his mind—images that made him want to vomit. He clenched his jaw, silencing his stomach. He couldn’t give in now. His claws dug into the ground, nails tearing through the earth in frustration. He had to stay hidden. He had to survive. Rakshasi was the only reason he wasn’t dead already. The human wouldn’t kill him as long as the dragoness was still fighting.

But Rakshasi’s ferocity had diminished. Her movements were sluggish, drained. The human easily blocked her attacks and countered with precision. Should Dion try to escape? Where could he go? If the human discovered he was missing, he’d return for him—certain death. He couldn’t leave Rakshasi. He had to act, but with his eyes closed and no immediate way to strike without being killed. Each time she was hit, the fire in his chest flared higher—no longer a spark, but a raging inferno. When he could finally move, when he could see, he would unleash everything. A heavy thud vibrated through the ground, followed by a smaller impact. Liquid splashed nearby. He couldn’t tell which was which, but he feared the worst. Then, the human laughed again—confirmation of his dread. He heard a wet, struggling kick, then another heavy thud on the earth.

Suddenly, Dion’s eyes snapped open. He looked around. Rakshasi lay on her back, drenched in blood and lacerations. Her chainmail was nearly gone, reduced to tattered strips. Blood seeped from her mouth. The sight was unbearable. “May Satan greet you, beast,” the human said, raising his sword for the final strike.

Squirrels are small to medium-sized rodents belonging to the family Sciuridae, recognized for their prominent tails and swift, coordinated movements. They inhabit a broad spectrum of environments, including forests, grasslands, and urban landscapes, and primarily consume plant-based foods such as seeds, nuts, and fruits. With over 200 recognized species globally, they are grouped into three main categories: tree squirrels, ground squirrels, and flying squirrels—each equipped with specialized traits suited to their specific habitats.

Ecologically, squirrels are vital contributors to their environments. Their habit of caching food plays a significant role in seed dispersal, fostering new plant growth and supporting forest recovery. They also form an essential link in food chains, serving as prey for numerous predators and helping maintain ecological balance.

To survive harsh winters, many squirrels gather and store food during the summer and fall months, relying on these caches when resources become limited. Some species, particularly certain ground squirrels, undergo hibernation, drastically lowering their metabolic activity to endure the cold season with minimal energy expenditure.

Although often cherished for their lively behavior, squirrels can occasionally become problematic in urban settings. They may chew on electrical wiring or take up residence in attics, leading to property damage. Nonetheless, such conflicts can typically be reduced through effective prevention strategies and responsible coexistence practices.

Spinach is a commonly consumed vegetable by both humans and animals, and many bird species are known to eat a variety of foods such as fruits, seeds, and insects. Bird owners often wonder whether spinach is safe for their pets. The answer is yes—birds can safely eat spinach when included as part of a balanced diet. Proper feeding practices are essential to ensure birds receive the benefits without risk. Below is a detailed guide on how to incorporate spinach into a bird’s diet.

Is Spinach Safe For Birds?  
Spinach is safe and beneficial for birds. It is rich in essential nutrients including Vitamin C, Vitamin A, calcium, potassium, manganese, and iron, all of which support healthy blood cells, metabolic processes, and overall well-being. Its high content of vitamins and minerals makes it an excellent addition to a bird’s daily diet. Additionally, spinach is easily digestible and provides energy-boosting nutrients. While birds generally enjoy leafy greens like spinach, they may not always show interest. In such cases, other safe vegetables can be offered as alternatives.

What Birds Eat Spinach?  
Numerous bird species consume spinach, though an exact count is not available. Research suggests at least 37 species include spinach in their diet. These include parrots, toucans, swifts, canaries, budgies, parakeets, and others. Parrots benefit greatly from spinach due to its high nutrient density, omega-3 fatty acids, and low fat content. Budgies particularly gain advantages from vitamin A, which supports vision, hearing, and bone health, along with vitamins C, E, and calcium. Parakeets also enjoy spinach, which provides vitamins A, B, C, and K. Swifts can eat spinach in moderation, but due to its high oxalate content, excessive intake may lead to health issues, so it should not be fed daily. It is crucial to wash spinach thoroughly to remove pesticides, as unwashed leaves can be harmful.

How To Feed Spinach To Birds?  
There are several effective ways to feed spinach to birds. One method is to place fresh, clean spinach leaves directly on an outdoor feeder or on the ground. Another approach is to create a spinach salad using chopped vegetables and place it in a birdhouse or near feeders, encouraging natural foraging behavior. A step-by-step method includes: filling a bowl with clean water, placing spinach in the center, and slowly adding warm water to just cover the leaves. Birds will be attracted to this setup. After feeding, any leftover spinach should be removed to prevent spoilage.

How Often & How Much To Feed Birds Spinach?  
The recommended daily amount of spinach for birds ranges from half an ounce to one ounce, depending on species and individual dietary needs. However, birds have difficulty digesting large amounts of cellulose, which is abundant in leafy greens like spinach. Overfeeding can lead to intestinal blockages from undigested plant matter. For birds with sensitive digestive systems, iceberg lettuce may be a better alternative due to its lower nutrient density but easier digestibility.

How Do I Get My Bird To Eat Spinach?  
Many birds resist green vegetables, but there are strategies to encourage consumption. Mixing finely chopped spinach with other nutritious foods such as seeds or oats can make it more appealing. Serving spinach in a different form, like mixed into pasta or pizza, may also help. Using food coloring to disguise the green color is a more advanced tactic that may work for some birds but not all. Spraying water on the spinach when the bird approaches can help them detect the scent through their beak, potentially increasing interest.

Can Birds Eat Raw Spinach?  
Yes, many bird species can eat raw spinach, provided it is properly prepared. Raw spinach should be thoroughly washed to remove contaminants and pesticides. While some birds may benefit from raw spinach as part of a varied diet, it should not be the sole source of nutrition. Cooking is not necessary for most birds, but the key is ensuring the spinach is clean and free from harmful residues.

Can Cockatiels Eat Spinach?  
Cockatiels can safely eat spinach. As primarily seed-eating birds, they thrive on a diet of high-quality parrot seed mix, fresh fruits, vegetables, and occasional treats like unsalted nuts or grated cheese. Spinach provides valuable nutrients such as calcium and vitamin A, which support strong bones, vision, and overall health. Cockatiels often enjoy spinach and other vegetables like apples and tomatoes, making it a suitable and nutritious addition to their meals.

Can Parakeets Eat Spinach?  
Parakeets naturally feed on small seeds and grains, but they readily accept dark leafy greens like spinach. They enjoy eating spinach both in whole leaf form and chopped, and it is considered one of their favorite vegetables. Spinach offers essential vitamins and minerals, including A, B, C, and K, contributing to their strength and vitality. As with all birds, spinach should be fresh, clean, and properly washed before serving.

Final Thoughts  
Spinach is a safe and nutritious food for many bird species when fed appropriately. It supports health through its rich vitamin and mineral content, but should be given in moderation and with proper preparation. Always ensure spinach is clean and free from pesticides. Birds benefit from dietary variety, and incorporating spinach into their meals can enhance their well-being. Feeding practices should be tailored to the species and individual bird’s preferences and needs. Córdoba and the Names of Nowhere  
The names of nowhere inscribe themselves in vanished tongues,  
entire poetic traditions, complete systems of language and gesture,  
etched into the waters of history, now dissolved  
into the fog of speculation, swept away by wind  
and the unraveling patterns of speech.  
Occasionally, nowhere mounts itself and sets out  
in search of nouns. Dressed in a red dress and white ribbons,  
it climbs into its engine-powered motion and drifts through the connotations  
of unseen cities—Canemah, Ocuri, Atlantis—singing  
a cycle of lost songs, fleeting epics.  
Hear the name the city bore before the reconquista—Qurtuba, Qurtuba—  
the cathedral rising on the site of a former mosque,  
rituals etched into stone at specific hours of the day,  
carved by a deity left stunned, unable to believe  
what has become of its creation.  
Hear the names of gods without worship,  
the rootless, the unnamed, moving in and out  
of places where no one remembers them—  
except for forgotten angels whispering a secret  
no one can hear but the wind, bound to the tongues of stone.  

The Palaver of Place  
Every landscape possesses its own palaver—  
the contours of slopes and elevations,  
the placement of grasses and trees, their textures  
and hues, their language of light and shadow,  
the way morning awakens and speaks itself,  
a moment of realization, a mode of existence,  
a way of seeing that carries the day into culture,  
a framework of attitudes, a feeling of belonging.  
A river declares, Let’s go.  
I’ve traveled far  
from where mountains scrape the sky and firs filter  
the clouds from the rain.  
I will go as far as I can, the river says,  
and then either join companions  
or gather around my own currents  
and form pools of stillness.  
Roads understand much about the land.  
They follow its flow along streams.  
Streets are less attuned.  
They insist on straight lines  
and aim to become intersections,  
defying the natural curves of the terrain.  
At times, when steps rise to meet porches,  
we glimpse how the land once rose,  
how hollows once held rain,  
how creeks once flowed before being trapped beneath concrete,  
now seeping occasionally into basements  
just to say, hey.  
Tim Barnes teaches creative writing, literature, and composition at Portland Community College. His most recent poetry collection is Definitions for a Lost Language. He co-edited Wood Works: The Life and Writings of Charles Erskine Scott Wood and currently edits the Friends of William Stafford newsletter.

A new study challenges the widely held belief that increasing competition for research funding and implementing top-down university management lead to better science. Across 17 countries, the research finds that while higher overall spending on research and development is strongly linked to greater production of high-quality science—specifically, papers in the top 10% most cited—increasing competition for funding does not improve scientific quality. In fact, the level of competitiveness in funding is negatively correlated with research quality. Similarly, greater top-down control over universities does not enhance efficiency or scientific output.

The study highlights that international comparisons of research performance based solely on the ratio of public R&D spending to the number of published articles are misleading. Significant differences in how countries structure their research systems—such as how PhDs are funded, how facilities are financed, and how budgets are administered—make direct spending comparisons unreliable. Even though R&D expenditure data are intended to be standardized globally, practical inconsistencies undermine their usefulness for cross-national benchmarking.

To address this, the researchers propose an alternative method: analyzing the relationship between changes in R&D spending and changes in high-quality scientific output, specifically the number of top 10% cited papers produced per additional unit of funding. This approach avoids the distortions caused by structural differences between national systems. While the data are imperfect, they allow for meaningful questioning of long-standing policy assumptions and support the exploration of alternative theoretical models.

The findings indicate that nearly 70% of the variation in highly cited scientific output across countries can be attributed to differences in overall funding levels, reinforcing the idea that more money leads to better science. The remaining 30% of variation must be explained by other factors, including the proportion of competitive versus core funding, whether core funding is tied to performance, the degree of university autonomy, and the extent of academic freedom.

Current science policy largely rests on three assumptions: that competitive funding drives better research, that performance-based institutional funding improves overall performance, and that greater managerial autonomy enhances efficiency. These principles have led to rising shares of competitive project funding and increased institutional freedom to manage budgets and strategies in many countries. However, the study finds no support for these assumptions.

Instead, the data show that higher levels of competitive funding are associated with lower efficiency in generating high-quality research. Countries like the UK and Finland, which rely heavily on competitive grants, gain fewer top papers per additional dollar spent compared to countries like the Netherlands and Spain, which provide more stable, non-competitive institutional funding. Furthermore, nations with retrospective national research evaluation systems—where expert panels assess research performance over the past five years—demonstrate higher efficiency.

Contrary to common belief, university autonomy does not improve research efficiency. Financial autonomy, measured by how much control universities have over their long-term budgets, shows no positive correlation with research performance. Other forms of autonomy—over staffing, teaching, governance, and work environment—are actually negatively correlated with efficiency. The more autonomy institutions have in these areas, the smaller the gains from increased research spending.

The researchers suggest this may stem from a trade-off between managerial power and academic freedom. As universities gain more autonomy, decision-making power often shifts from faculty to administrators, potentially undermining researchers’ freedom to choose topics and methods. Limited available data on academic freedom support a negative relationship between academic freedom and managerial autonomy, which may in turn reduce research quality.

Efficient science systems, according to the findings, are characterized by retrospective evaluation of past research, substantial institutional funding, and limited managerial autonomy. In contrast, less efficient systems emphasize control through high levels of competitive project funding—which dictates what research is done—and strong top-down management, which controls even more aspects of university operations.

While the conclusions are based on limited and imperfect data, and further research across more countries and with broader measures of impact is needed, the study strongly suggests that current science policy is not evidence-based. The prevailing model, which prioritizes competition and managerial control, may not only be ineffective but potentially harmful to scientific progress. The characteristics identified in high-performing systems—stable funding, past-oriented evaluation, and restrained managerial power—offer a more promising foundation for future science policy.

This is an unusual topic, but have you ever felt a wave of disgust watching someone in a public space intensely picking their nose? It’s as if they’re searching for treasure, completely unaware of how off-putting it appears. And just when you think it can’t get worse, they bring that same finger to their mouth and consume whatever they’ve collected. This behavior is undeniably revolting and highly unhygienic—yet it’s surprisingly common.

From a medical standpoint, this habit has a specific name: rhinotillexis, which refers to the act of picking one’s nose. When the mucus or nasal debris is then ingested, the term mucophagy applies. The existence of formal medical terminology for these behaviors suggests they are not rare or isolated incidents.

One particularly controversial claim comes from Dr. Friedrich Bischinger, an Austrian lung specialist, who actually advocates for nose picking and eating boogers in children. He argues that using a finger allows access to areas unreachable by tissues, resulting in a cleaner nasal passage. He further claims that consuming the dried nasal secretions strengthens the immune system, likening it to a natural form of immunization—similar to a flu shot. According to him, this exposure to bacteria and germs helps the body develop defenses against illness. While this idea may sound extreme, it’s rooted in the theory that controlled exposure to microbes can promote immune resilience. Still, most medical professionals strongly disagree. They maintain that the most effective way to stay healthy is to avoid exposure to pathogens altogether, not invite them in through such means.

There are legitimate health risks associated with nose picking. Our hands are among the most germ-laden parts of the body, having come into contact with countless surfaces—doorknobs, phones, shared devices—throughout the day. These surfaces harbor bacteria and viruses. When you pick your nose with unwashed hands, you’re directly transferring those pathogens into your nasal cavity, a warm, moist, and dark environment ideal for microbial growth. This increases the risk of infection and illness.

Additionally, aggressive nose picking can cause physical damage. Scratching or tearing the delicate mucous membranes inside the nose can lead to bleeding. If a blood vessel is ruptured, pathogens can enter the bloodstream directly. Given the proximity of the nasal cavity to the brain, there’s a potential for serious complications. One such risk is cavernous sinus thrombosis—a rare but dangerous condition involving blood clots in the sinuses near the brain, often linked to infections from facial boils or trauma. While nose picking isn’t a common direct cause, the risk of introducing infection into this sensitive area is real.

There’s also a widespread myth that nose picking can puncture the brain. This is medically impossible. Even if someone were to push their finger as far as possible into the nasal passage, it would not reach the brain. The finger would first pass through the nasal cavity, then enter the sinuses—air-filled spaces behind the nose and cheeks. Beyond that lies the cribriform plate, a thin bony structure forming part of the ethmoid bone in the skull. This acts as a natural barrier, preventing any finger from reaching the brain. So despite the intense focus some people apply, the brain remains safely out of reach.

While the habit is nearly universal—most people have picked their nose at some point—there’s no need to start doing it. If it’s necessary, it should be done discreetly and in private. Practicing good hygiene is crucial: washing hands before and after the act can significantly reduce the risk of introducing harmful microbes. In short, while the idea of boosting immunity through nose picking may sound intriguing to a few, the potential health risks and social stigma make it a practice best avoided.

Anxiety is a widespread concern impacting individuals across society. It can affect anyone at any time, and college students often encounter test anxiety, which may lead to writing an essay on the subject. If you're tasked with composing a test anxiety essay, you might feel uncertain about where to start. This article provides a proven essay outline and practical advice to help you produce a strong, well-structured paper. Continue reading to gain deeper insight.

Key strategies for writing a test anxiety essay:

- Review existing essays on test anxiety  
Engaging with various sources broadens your understanding of the topic and strengthens your approach to writing. Seek out credible, verified materials focused on test anxiety to gain a solid foundation of knowledge and identify essential elements to include in your own essay.

- Study essays that discuss reducing test anxiety  
When addressing anxiety in your paper, it’s important to offer meaningful solutions. Readers often look for practical strategies to manage anxiety. By reviewing sample essays that focus on coping mechanisms, you can gather effective ideas and incorporate them into your own work.

- Choose a personal angle, such as "How I Overcame My Test Anxiety"  
Personalizing your essay can greatly enhance its authenticity and impact. Reflect on your own experiences with test anxiety—what triggered it, how you felt, and what steps helped you overcome it. Using real-life examples makes your argument more relatable and strengthens your discussion with genuine insight.

- Investigate effective ways to begin a test anxiety essay  
Every essay requires a strong opening that captures the reader’s attention. The introduction sets the tone and determines whether the reader will continue. Research different techniques for crafting compelling openings, such as using a relevant quote, a personal anecdote, or a startling statistic. If you're unsure, consult your instructor or peers who have previously written similar essays for guidance.

- Seek advice from your tutor on writing about test anxiety  
Don’t hesitate to reach out to your teacher for support. They are a valuable resource who can clarify expectations, help refine your thesis statement, and guide you through developing clear, coherent arguments in the main body. Talking to your tutor can prevent common mistakes and improve the overall quality of your essay.

- Develop a detailed essay outline  
Before writing, create a structured outline to organize your thoughts. This preliminary framework ensures a logical flow and prevents disorganized content. Your outline should include:

- Introduction: Present your understanding of anxiety, share your personal fears, and explain how anxiety has affected your life.
- Thesis statement: Clearly state the central argument or focus of your essay in a concise and direct manner.
- Main body: Break down your discussion into distinct paragraphs, each addressing a separate point related to test anxiety—such as causes, symptoms, effects, or coping strategies. Avoid repeating ideas across multiple paragraphs.
- Conclusion: Summarize the key points discussed throughout the essay and restate your thesis in a way that reinforces your argument.

Writing about anxiety is a common academic assignment in college. To ensure your essay stands out, aim for originality. Avoid copying content from online sources and rephrasing it as your own. Instead, draw from personal experiences and reflect deeply on the topic to craft a unique, thoughtful, and authentic paper.

Resveratrol is a naturally occurring compound found in certain foods such as grapes, nuts, and dark chocolate, and has demonstrated potential for supporting various aspects of health and wellness. It functions by activating a group of enzymes called Sirtuins, which are located in the mitochondria—the cellular structures responsible for energy production and metabolic regulation. Enhanced mitochondrial activity through Sirtuin activation contributes to improved cellular function, which in turn supports overall physical health and may help delay age-related decline.

As a flavonoid, a type of phytochemical, Resveratrol has been linked to protective effects against oxidative stress, cholesterol buildup, blood clots, and the development of certain tumors. Its ability to support cellular health may also extend to reducing the impact of underlying conditions that contribute to hair loss. Since hair follicles reside in the dermis—the skin’s inner layer—overall skin health plays a critical role in maintaining healthy hair growth. Resveratrol’s protective effects on skin, including defense against damage and aging, can support optimal follicle function and help prevent hair thinning and loss.

Research has shown that Resveratrol may improve cardiometabolic health by enhancing endothelial function, which refers to the health of the inner lining of blood vessels. Endothelial dysfunction is associated with reduced blood flow, vascular remodeling, and plaque rupture—conditions that can impair nutrient delivery to hair follicles and hinder hair growth. By promoting better circulation and reducing inflammation, Resveratrol may help mitigate these risks. Its anti-inflammatory properties are particularly relevant, as chronic inflammation is a known contributor to hair loss.

The potential benefits of Resveratrol include improved cardiovascular health, delayed onset and slowed progression of age-related conditions such as hair loss, enhanced metabolic function, better skin and follicle health, and reduced inflammation-related hair loss. However, due to its biological activity, Resveratrol also carries potential side effects. It exhibits anticoagulant-like properties, similar to Warfarin, and can influence estrogen activity in the body. These effects may pose risks for certain individuals, including women with hormone-sensitive cancers, those on contraceptives, pregnant or potentially pregnant women, people with platelet disorders, individuals with diabetes, and those with heart conditions. Therefore, it is essential to consult a healthcare provider before beginning any Resveratrol supplementation.

While supplements and prescription formulations are available, increasing Resveratrol intake through whole foods is a safer and often effective alternative. Natural dietary sources include dark chocolate with high cocoa content, blueberries, red grapes (especially the skins), and various nuts such as walnuts, pistachios, almonds, and cashews. Although peanut butter contains small amounts of Resveratrol, it is derived from legumes and may trigger allergic reactions in some people, potentially causing inflammation, so it is not recommended as a primary source.

A practical way to boost Resveratrol levels is through a nutrient-rich smoothie. This smoothie combines hemp protein, frozen or fresh blueberries, red seedless grapes, high-cocoa-content chocolate (70% or higher), mixed nuts, almond milk or water, coconut oil or flesh, and a splash of pumpkin seed oil for added benefit. Pumpkin seed oil has been clinically shown to increase hair count, making it a valuable addition. Consuming this smoothie at least once a week for a month can significantly elevate Resveratrol levels, with continued use as desired. As with any dietary change, moderation is key, and any adverse effects should prompt immediate consultation with a medical professional.
