RDS now offers the world’s most transparent and dependable displays, featuring built-in Lumineq Touch Technology. These displays leverage atomic layer deposition (ALD) to produce ultra-thin, nanometre-scale films, ensuring exceptional reliability and durability while maintaining full transparency. The Lumineq Transparent Thin Film Electroluminescent (TASEL) displays are constructed with a solid-state glass panel and an electronic control circuit. The panel includes a luminescent phosphor layer positioned between transparent dielectric layers and conductive indium tin oxide (ITO) electrodes. When voltage is applied to the electrodes, the intersecting pixel or segment emits light, enabling clear, visible display output.

The integration of touch functionality is achieved through an In-Cell PCAP (Projected Capacitive) design, where touch sensors are embedded directly within the existing functional layers of the display. This eliminates the need for additional layers, preserving the display’s thin profile, lightweight nature, and structural robustness. The touch-sensitive regions utilize the same ITO layers responsible for electroluminescence, ensuring seamless integration without compromising performance.

With this technology, any glass surface can be transformed into a touch-enabled interface. Applications are wide-ranging—from vehicles, where users could unlock doors, enter car-sharing codes, or adjust sunroof tint with a touch on a window, to homes and offices, where touch glass displays can serve as security keypads or access controls for rooms and workspaces. The potential uses are extensive, limited only by imagination. For further information, visit www.review-displays.co.uk.

If content doesn’t offer real value, it shouldn’t be considered content marketing. Today’s consumers actively avoid traditional ads, using tools like DVRs and ad blockers to skip them. This shift makes content marketing highly effective because it isn’t an ad—it prioritizes the audience by addressing their actual needs, interests, and pain points, contributing meaningful value to their lives rather than pushing a sales message. People now seek out content that provides solutions, entertainment, or practical tools that save time, while filtering out anything that feels irrelevant or tedious. If your current advertising fails to engage, wastes time, or only solves minor issues, content marketing offers a more effective alternative.

Successful content marketing connects with audiences by resonating, informing, entertaining, and even delighting them. It avoids the deceptive tactics of advertorials that disguise promotions as editorial content. Instead, it delivers value independent of your core offerings. In return, consumers grant you their attention—attention they typically withhold from conventional advertising. This leads to longer interactions with your brand and deeper engagement. It’s effective throughout the entire marketing funnel: generating leads by directing traffic to landing pages and websites, influencing consideration during brand evaluation, and building broad awareness. When done well, it can convert leads into a loyal subscription list, enabling ongoing marketing efforts with the same audience for years, simply by consistently delivering timely and relevant content.

Content marketing has existed for over a century and comes in many formats—blog posts, podcasts, ebooks, infographics, long- and short-form videos, documentaries, events, and print magazines. The key is that all impactful content marketing revolves around compelling stories or informative material. Creating high-quality content requires investment in time and resources, so planning for content repurposing is essential. A single piece of content—like a white paper—can be transformed into a video, a blog post can be broken into a series of social media updates, and so on. The best approach is to design a repurposing strategy before creating the original content.

Beyond audience engagement, content marketing offers several underappreciated benefits. It enhances SEO by increasing backlinks and incorporating relevant keywords across content. It also establishes your brand as a trusted authority in your industry—a significant advantage in building credibility and long-term customer relationships.

The solar water pumping system functions as an independent unit powered by photovoltaic (PV) technology. Solar cells convert sunlight into electricity, which drives a DC surface centrifugal mono-block pump to extract water from borewells, open wells, or water reservoirs for applications in irrigation and drinking water supply.

Key advantages of solar pump sets include:
- Zero fuel expenses, as they rely on freely available sunlight
- No need for connection to conventional grid electricity
- Extended operational lifespan
- High reliability and durability with consistent performance
- Simple operation and low maintenance requirements
- Reduction in the consumption of conventional diesel fuel

This paper aims to deepen the understanding of how new generation telecommunications systems evolve in large developing countries, focusing on the key dynamics that shape this process from the standpoint of inter-firm collaboration networks. By analyzing the development of collaborative networks within China's 3G mobile telecommunications sector, the study identifies that the motivation to exchange resources and expand experiential knowledge between domestic and foreign manufacturers—particularly in the context of internationalization—plays a significant role in driving the formation of inter-firm networks centered around a dominant design. The ability to effectively structure and coordinate these network configurations proves essential for latecomer firms seeking to compete in the global standard-setting race. Consequently, actively accessing external resources and securing central positions within the network significantly enhances the likelihood that local firms will achieve innovation capacity in the development of complex information systems. The research draws on the case of China’s 3G mobile telecommunications industry, emphasizing the strategic importance of network positioning and resource integration for technological advancement. The findings are relevant to the broader fields of collaboration networks, 3G mobile systems, commercialization, China, new generation telecommunications, local firms, and information systems. The article was published in the International Journal of Information Technology and Management, Volume 10, Issues 2/3/4, pages 151–166, in 2011, with the online publication date of September 18, 2011. The paper was received on May 8, 2021, and accepted on May 12, 2021.

Each year, over 4500 pregnancies in the European Union are affected by neural tube defects. Since 1991, there has been clear evidence that taking folic acid around the time of conception can prevent most neural tube defects, and improving folate levels could prevent more than two-thirds of cases. This study examines trends in the prevalence of neural tube defects up to 2001, alongside a survey of periconceptional folic acid policies and their implementation across 16 European countries.

Eurocat is a network of population-based congenital anomaly registries across Europe. The analysis included data from 31 registries in 16 countries covering 9,273,212 births between 1980 and 2001. Among these, 8,913 infants or fetuses were diagnosed with neural tube defects—specifically anencephaly, spina bifida, or encephalocele—comprising 3,298 live births, 844 stillbirths, and 4,771 pregnancies terminated after prenatal diagnosis. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the yearly prevalence of neural tube defects declined significantly from 45 per 10,000 births in 1980 to between 10 and 15 per 10,000 in the 1990s—an ongoing trend that began before any formal folic acid supplementation policies were introduced. In contrast, in the rest of Europe, prevalence remained consistently around 10 per 10,000 births throughout the 1980s and beyond.

The first countries to introduce periconceptional folic acid supplementation policies were the United Kingdom (1992), Ireland (1993), and the Netherlands (1993). Six additional countries followed: Switzerland (1996), Denmark (1997), Norway (1998), Portugal (1998), France (2000), and Spain (2001). Malta (1994) and Finland (1995) opted for dietary strategies alone to increase folate intake. Austria, Belgium, Croatia, Germany, and Italy had no national policy, though professional medical organizations in these countries issued guidelines.

For 23 registries with data available from at least 1990, the study compared changes in prevalence over time based on policy type. The ratio of prevalence in 1999–2001 to that in 1989–1991 was calculated for each registry, and the mean of these ratios—on a log scale—was determined using standard random effects meta-analysis techniques. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, a statistically significant overall reduction in neural tube defect prevalence was observed between 1999–2001 and 1989–1991 (32% reduction, 95% confidence interval 17% to 44%), consistent with a trend that predates policy implementation. Registries in countries with policies introduced by 1999 to increase periconceptional folate levels—through supplementation or dietary means—showed a mean reduction of 17% (ranging from a 44% decrease to a 4% increase). In contrast, registries from countries without a policy by 1999 showed a mean reduction of only 9% (ranging from a 26% decrease to a 12% increase).

Despite national folic acid supplementation policies in half of the European countries, the overall prevalence of neural tube defects in Europe has not declined substantially over the past decade. The 32% reduction in the UK and Ireland reflects a stronger pre-existing downward trend and leaves their prevalence slightly above the European average. These findings suggest that policies relying solely on recommending periconceptional folic acid supplementation for planned pregnancies are insufficient. Many women may not receive or act on health messages urging them to start supplementation before conception, or may be unaware that dietary changes alone are unlikely to achieve adequate folate levels. Moreover, a significant proportion of pregnancies in most countries are unplanned. Raising folate levels across the population through the fortification of staple foods with folic acid could ensure broader coverage before conception and help reduce socioeconomic disparities in neural tube defect rates. Health outcomes related to supplementation and fortification should be monitored, and policies should be periodically reviewed based on emerging evidence. The potential to prevent neural tube defects in Europe through improved folate status remains largely unrealized, and it is unacceptable to continue depending primarily on prenatal screening and pregnancy termination as the main strategies for reducing the number of affected births.

What is already known: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation can prevent most neural tube defects when widely used, but it must begin before conception to be effective.

What this study adds: The lack of a significant decline in neural tube defect prevalence across Europe since 1991 indicates that the full preventive potential has not been achieved. Effective strategies must include both periconceptional supplementation and mandatory fortification of staple foods to reach all women before conception and prevent the widening of socioeconomic inequalities in birth defect rates.

Students engage in a data-driven problem-solving activity using an Excel spreadsheet containing batting averages for players on the Baltimore Orioles. The lesson aims to develop students’ ability to use statistical data to predict trends and make informed generalizations. The activity requires access to computers with Excel, the Orioles' Batting Averages spreadsheet, an assessment rubric, a teacher computer equipped with a projector, and a printer capable of handling legal-size paper (8 ½” x 14”).

Prior to the lesson, the teacher downloads the associated spreadsheet and ensures it is available on student computers. The teacher also prepares the classroom setup with a projector to display the spreadsheet during instruction. Students will later print their revised spreadsheets on legal-size paper, so this detail must be emphasized.

The lesson begins with a discussion about baseball or softball, focusing on how coaches determine batting line-ups. Students reflect on the importance of batting order and consider whether it can influence a team’s success. The teacher then introduces the objective: using a spreadsheet with formulas to calculate batting averages, analyze player performance, and create a new, data-supported batting order.

The teacher reviews the calculation of batting averages using sample problems on the board while students work through them on paper. For example, if a player has 2 hits in 4 at-bats, their average is 2 divided by 4, resulting in .500. If another player has 2 hits in 6 at-bats, their average is 2 divided by 6, or .333. The teacher emphasizes that even with the same number of hits, a higher number of at-bats lowers the average, illustrating the importance of both hits and opportunities. Additional examples are provided to ensure students grasp the concept and can calculate averages independently.

Using the projector and the Orioles' Batting Averages spreadsheet, the teacher demonstrates the structure of the spreadsheet, explaining how columns are labeled with letters and rows with numbers, allowing users to locate any cell. The teacher highlights data entries for each game, including at-bats and hits. The class then examines the formula used to calculate the batting average in the “Average” column. The teacher points out that formulas appear in the formula bar above the spreadsheet, starting with an equals sign and involving cell references and division operations. By clicking on different players’ averages, the teacher shows how the formulas vary based on the specific data points used.

The teacher selects one player and tracks their performance across games, discussing how their batting average reflects their consistency. Students are asked whether the number of at-bats affects the batting order and why. They are also prompted to identify the most consistent batter and justify their choice. The class discusses where in the batting order consistent performers should be placed.

The teacher guides students to the total batting average summary section, where overall averages are displayed. Students analyze trends to determine which players are improving over the season and which are declining, considering possible causes such as injuries or slumps. They are then asked to evaluate the current batting order, offering suggestions for improvement and supporting their reasoning with data.

Additional observations about the data are invited from students. The teacher then demonstrates how to update the batting order and input predictions for game six, including estimated hits and at-bats. Students are allowed to change the team name by editing the title and modifying the formula bar. The teacher organizes students into pairs or small groups, ensuring each has access to a computer. As students work, the teacher circulates to provide formative assessment, offer help to struggling learners, and monitor progress.

Students input their revised batting order and enter predictions for game six. The spreadsheet automatically recalculates the batting averages using the existing formulas. Each student then writes a paragraph explaining their reasoning for the new batting order and their predictions for future performance. They save their work under their name using the “Save As” function and print their spreadsheet on legal-size paper. The printed spreadsheet is attached to the written rationale and submitted to the teacher.

Throughout the activity, the teacher supports students by answering questions and asking clarifying questions to deepen understanding. Mastery is assessed using the printed revised spreadsheet and the written rationale, evaluated against the provided assessment rubric. The lesson can be adapted to other sports, allowing students to design their own spreadsheets and learn how to construct formulas based on desired outcomes.

ROJAS, Juan et al. Antihypertensive effect and lethal dose 50 of Passiflora edulis leaves (maracuya) fruit juice and ethanolic extract in rats. An. Fac. med. [online]. 2006, vol.67, n.3, pp. 206-213. ISSN 1025-5583.

Objectives: To evaluate the antihypertensive effect and determine the lethal dose 50 (LD50) of fruit juice and ethanolic extract derived from Passiflora edulis leaves in rats.  
Design: A prospective, analytical-experimental, preclinical in vivo study.  
Setting: Faculties of Medicine, Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, and Pharmacy and Biochemistry, Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos.  
Biological material: Rats.  
Interventions: Four groups of six rats each were used to assess the antihypertensive effect. Following baseline blood pressure measurement, arterial hypertension was induced in all animals via oral administration of L-NAME at 50 mg/kg/day. Two days after induction, treatment began with distilled water, ethanolic extract (500 mg/kg/day), fruit juice (500 mg/kg/day), or captopril (100 mg/kg/day), all administered orally. Blood pressure was measured on days 3, 4, 7, and 10. For LD50 determination, 12 groups of ten mice each were used, with seven different dose levels of the ethanolic extract and five dose levels for the fruit juice.  
Main outcome measures: Reduction in blood pressure.  
Results: Both the ethanolic extract and fruit juice significantly reduced systolic blood pressure (SBP) from the first day of treatment, with values of 157.2 ± 2.3 mmHg and 156.2 ± 2.1 mmHg, respectively, compared to 167.7 ± 1.7 mmHg in the L-NAME control group (p < 0.005 and p < 0.001, respectively). Diastolic blood pressure (DBP) also showed significant reduction starting on the first day of treatment. The LD50 for the ethanolic extract was determined to be 10,687 mg/kg, and for the fruit juice, it was 21,471 mg/kg.  
Conclusions: The ethanolic extract of Passiflora edulis leaves and its fruit juice effectively reduce arterial blood pressure in hypertensive rats and demonstrate no acute oral toxicity at the tested doses.  
Keywords: Passiflora edulis; hypertension; research

The concept discussed here was applied in an analysis of 'free will' originally published on a usenet news group and now accessible online. The analysis highlights that examining different kinds of architectural designs—whether intentionally created or evolved in response to environmental pressures—reveals a limitation in using simple binary distinctions to describe design types. A key insight from this approach is that designing, testing, and refining complex systems often uncovers a far greater diversity of internal states than initially anticipated.

Systems featuring complex virtual machines with multiple interacting, concurrent subsystems—some of which monitor or regulate others—can exhibit internal dynamics that cannot be fully captured by observing external behavior or input-output relationships. For instance, such systems may operate internally without any connection to external inputs or outputs for extended periods, only occasionally engaging with the outside world. A clear example is a sophisticated virtual machine capable of playing various games, which may internally simulate games like chess or draughts (checkers) through self-play. This internal practice enhances its skill, yet no external indication of these changes occurs unless it interacts with an external player—an event that may never happen.

By analyzing the full range of internal states enabled by a system's information-processing architecture, we may discover that understanding its functioning requires a far more elaborate ontology of states and processes than what can be inferred from observable behavior alone. Even if input and output channels are limited, restricting the number of games actually played over a lifetime, the system may still possess the underlying competence to engage in many more. This is especially true of humans: our everyday language concepts for mental processes, as well as those developed by psychologists and psychiatrists through observation and experimentation, may not be sufficient to account for the full depth and complexity of human cognition and experience. A richer ontology—grounded in a robust theoretical understanding of how such systems function—is necessary. This parallels the historical shift in science when the discovery of atomic and molecular structures revolutionized our understanding of matter, revealing forms and interactions that were previously unimaginable.

These themes are further explored in various papers from the Cognition and Affect project and the CoSy Robot project. A particularly relevant methodological paper, titled "Two Notions Contrasted: 'Logical Geography' and 'Logical Topography'", examines the distinction between two approaches to conceptual analysis. It builds on Gilbert Ryle's idea of 'Logical Geography'—the mapping of existing concepts and their relationships—by introducing 'Logical Topography', which investigates the underlying structural possibilities of reality that enable certain kinds of concepts to emerge. Unlike 'Logical Geography', which assumes a fixed set of concepts and a single definitive way of charting them, 'Logical Topography' recognizes that reality can be segmented in multiple ways, each giving rise to different conceptual frameworks. It also reveals that reality may contain hidden structural complexity, which, when thoroughly explored, uncovers possibilities previously obscured by conventional philosophical inquiry.

This approach to theory-building shares strong parallels with scientific theory development, including the capacity to expand our ontology through abduction—the inference to the best explanation. It emphasizes the importance of exploring underlying mechanisms rather than relying solely on current conceptual schemes.

The ideas presented here were first introduced in 2005. Some related work includes "Prolegomena to a Theory of Communication and Affect," which outlines several approaches to studying the mind: the design-based, phenomena-based, and semantics-based approaches. An additional approach, the mechanism-based one, starts from assumed mechanisms—such as neural networks—and attempts to explain observed or introspected mental phenomena. Daniel Dennett’s "intentional stance," also known as the "knowledge level" in Herbert Simon and Allen Newell’s framework, assumes rationality in the system being studied. However, this assumption is neither justified nor necessary when analyzing biological information-processing systems like humans, ants, or microbes.

The design-based approach aligns closely with the study of logical topography, as it focuses on understanding how systems work and how alternative designs might function. It is related to Dennett’s "design stance," particularly in interpretations that emphasize understanding how systems operate and how similar systems could be constructed. However, there is another interpretation of the design stance—where one assumes a system has been designed (by evolution or otherwise) to perform a certain function and uses that to predict behavior—without delving into internal workings. This latter interpretation does not fully capture the design-based approach, which prioritizes deep mechanistic understanding. Dennett appears to have shifted between these two interpretations.

The term "designer stance," as used by John McCarthy, is closely aligned with the design-based approach described here. This connection is elaborated in footnote 5 of his paper "The Well-Designed Child," originally drafted in 1996 and published in the Artificial Intelligence journal in 2008, alongside his related work "The Well-Designed Young Mathematician" in the context of philosophy of mathematics and young robots.

Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a bacterium that can infect the stomach and upper part of the small intestine. It is associated with a range of gastrointestinal conditions, including gastritis, peptic ulcers, and an increased risk of stomach cancer. Many infections are asymptomatic or cause only mild symptoms, and in such cases, the prognosis is excellent. When symptoms are present and treatment is administered appropriately, the outlook remains favorable, though up to 20% of patients may experience a recurrence of the infection. Individuals with ulcers who successfully eradicate the bacterium typically heal well, often with only minor tissue scarring.

Untreated, severe infections can lead to serious complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, significant scarring, anemia, and hypotension (low blood pressure), which can be life-threatening if not addressed promptly. The prognosis for these cases is therefore more guarded.

Diagnosis of H. pylori infection can be achieved through various methods, including breath tests, stool antigen tests, and endoscopic biopsies. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a breath test specifically for use in children. Treatment typically involves a combination of antibiotics and acid-suppressing medications, such as proton pump inhibitors, to eliminate the bacteria and promote healing.

Treatment is recommended for individuals with peptic ulcers, those with a history of gastric cancer, people with certain types of stomach inflammation, and those with unexplained iron deficiency anemia or who are on long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). While the exact mode of transmission is not fully understood, H. pylori is believed to spread through oral-oral or fecal-oral routes, suggesting it may be contagious, particularly in environments with poor sanitation.

Prevention strategies are limited but may include maintaining good hygiene practices and safe food and water handling. The overall prognosis for H. pylori infection is generally positive when detected and treated early, especially in comparison to untreated or advanced cases. The information presented is supported by guidelines from the American College of Gastroenterology, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the National Cancer Institute, and other authoritative medical sources.

To understand balance sheets fully, focus on how they change over time. Examine shifts in asset composition and fluctuations in liabilities. These changes reveal a company’s strategic choices and the effectiveness of its financial management. When working on a financial reporting assignment, use the balance sheet to evaluate a company’s financial condition. Analyze how the balance among assets, liabilities, and equity influences its resilience during economic shifts. Apply financial ratios such as the debt-to-equity ratio to quantify insights derived from the balance sheet. Select a specific company, review its balance sheets across multiple periods, and identify trends. Assess how changes in assets and liabilities reflect growth, investment, or operational challenges. This practical approach strengthens your grasp of how balance sheets are used in real-world financial analysis.

Mastering the interpretation of balance sheets gives you a deeper understanding of a company’s financial structure and overall health. As you continue your financial reporting work, remember that the balance sheet acts as a guiding tool, helping you navigate the complexities of a company’s financial situation.

Moving forward, focus on the cash flow statement, a key element that clarifies a company’s liquidity. While income statements and balance sheets report on earnings and financial position, the cash flow statement tracks actual cash movements within the business. It functions as a dynamic roadmap, showing cash inflows and outflows over a defined period.

The cash flow statement is organized into three main sections, each providing distinct insights:

Operating Activities: This section shows the cash generated or used in everyday business operations.

Investing Activities: It includes cash spent on long-term assets like property, plant, and equipment, as well as proceeds from selling such assets or investments in securities.

Financing Activities: This captures cash flows related to owners and creditors, such as issuing or buying back stock, paying dividends, borrowing money, or repaying loans.

Understanding the cash flow statement is essential for evaluating a company’s liquidity—the ability to meet short-term financial commitments. Positive cash flow from operations suggests strong core business performance, whereas persistent negative cash flow may indicate financial strain.

By analyzing the cash flow statement, you can uncover the reasoning behind a company’s financial decisions. For example, increased borrowing may signal expansion plans, while heavy spending on capital projects could reflect growth ambitions. Tracing the flow of cash helps reveal the strategic direction shaping the company’s financial profile.

In your financial reporting assignments, use the cash flow statement to complement information from the income statement and balance sheet. A company may report high profits but still struggle with cash shortages if operating cash flow is negative. To deepen your understanding, pick a company and study its cash flow statements over time. Assess how operational choices affect cash flow and look for recurring patterns. This real-world application enhances your appreciation of how cash flow analysis informs financial decision-making.

By becoming skilled at following the cash trail, you develop a refined understanding of a company’s liquidity, financial choices, and overall financial stability. As you work through financial reporting tasks, remember that the cash flow statement serves as a critical guide through the evolving financial landscape of a business.

Next, explore financial ratios—the essential tools of financial analysis. These metrics act like a detective’s magnifying glass, enabling you to examine a company’s performance, efficiency, and profitability in detail.

Financial ratios are designed to highlight relationships between different elements of financial statements, offering a focused view of a company’s health. They help identify strengths, weaknesses, and trends that might not be apparent from raw numbers alone.

Common types of financial ratios include:

Liquidity Ratios: These assess a company’s ability to meet short-term obligations. Key examples are the current ratio and quick ratio, which measure short-term financial flexibility.

Profitability Ratios: These evaluate how effectively a company generates profits relative to revenue, assets, or equity. Important metrics include net profit margin, return on assets (ROA), and return on equity (ROE).

Efficiency Ratios: These analyze how well a company uses its assets and liabilities. Examples include inventory turnover, receivables turnover, and asset turnover, all of which reflect operational efficiency.

Leverage Ratios: These examine the level of debt a company carries and its capacity to meet long-term financial commitments. The debt-to-equity ratio and interest coverage ratio are central to assessing financial leverage.

Market Ratios: These reflect investor sentiment and market valuation. The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and earnings per share (EPS) connect a company’s financial results to its stock price.

Use ratios strategically, much like a detective investigates clues. For instance, a high current ratio may suggest strong liquidity, but when paired with low efficiency ratios, it might indicate poor asset utilization. Combining ratio analysis with data from income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements provides a comprehensive view of a company’s financial condition.

In your financial reporting assignments, integrate ratio analysis to deliver a well-rounded evaluation. Track how ratios evolve over time and interpret what these changes reveal about performance and strategy. With this knowledge, financial reporting tasks transform from challenging assignments into meaningful opportunities to demonstrate your analytical skills. This guide equips you to interpret financial statements, analyze balance sheets, cash flow statements, and apply ratios effectively. Proficiency in Excel enhances data handling and reporting efficiency. As you continue your financial journey, refer to this guide as a reliable resource. Approach each assignment with confidence, knowing you have the tools to succeed.

Mr Burger, a fast-food chain once prevalent across west Texas, eastern New Mexico, and western Oklahoma, is remembered by some as the worst burger chain ever. Though its peak popularity occurred in the 1970s, the chain remained operational in certain small towns into the early 1990s. Modeled after the Texas Dairy Queen concept—featuring a location in nearly every small town across the Texas panhandle—Mr Burger diverged significantly in quality. While Dairy Queens were known for reliable service and consistent offerings, Mr Burger's food was consistently poor: fries were cold, burgers lacked flavor, and side dishes were unremarkable and forgettable. Despite this, the question remains whether anyone, even faintly, holds a positive recollection of these establishments.

Java is a prominent programming language in software development and is particularly effective for building applications with AWS SQS. Its mature ecosystem and strong community support empower developers to create scalable, dependable systems that integrate smoothly with SQS. The official AWS SDK for Java offers extensive libraries and APIs, simplifying interaction with SQS.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) complements SQS and is frequently used alongside it. SNS facilitates message publishing and subscription, delivering a flexible, highly scalable messaging mechanism. When combined with SQS, it supports the creation of robust event-driven architectures and enhances component decoupling.

Docker, a leading containerization platform, enables developers to package applications with their dependencies into lightweight, portable containers. When used with AWS SQS, Docker helps establish scalable, isolated environments for distributed systems, streamlining the deployment and management of applications that depend on SQS for message queuing.

The Serverless Framework is a widely used open-source tool for developing serverless applications. It simplifies the definition, deployment, and management of AWS resources—including SQS—through a straightforward configuration file. This framework allows developers to implement event-driven architectures and connect their applications to SQS without managing underlying infrastructure.

Amazon CloudWatch is a monitoring and observability service that provides visibility into the performance and operational health of AWS resources. When integrated with SQS, CloudWatch enables tracking of message counts, queue activity, and the setup of alarms for detecting issues or anomalies. This integration helps maintain the consistent and reliable operation of SQS-based applications.

Advantages of AWS SQS:
- Scalability: SQS supports effortless scaling to meet growing application demands, handling an unlimited number of messages with high throughput.
- Durability: Messages are redundantly stored across multiple availability zones within a region, ensuring high durability and resilience against failures.
- Reliability: As a managed service, SQS handles the complexities of message queuing and ensures dependable message delivery.
- Decoupling: SQS promotes loose coupling between application components, allowing asynchronous communication, improved fault tolerance, and independent scaling.
- Message Types: Supports standard messages, FIFO (First-In-First-Out) messages, and message groups, offering flexibility for diverse message handling needs.
- Visibility Timeout: Allows control over how long a message remains invisible to other consumers after being retrieved, reducing duplication and ensuring reliable processing.
- Delay Queues: Enables setting a delay before messages become available for processing, useful for staggering message processing or implementing time-based workflows.
- AWS Integration: Seamlessly connects with other AWS services such as Lambda, EC2, and SNS, supporting the development of scalable, distributed systems.
- Cost Efficiency: Operates on a pay-as-you-go model, charging only for the number of messages and API requests used, making it economical for applications of all sizes.

Disadvantages of AWS SQS:
- Message Ordering: While SQS offers best-effort ordering, strict message sequencing cannot be guaranteed. Applications requiring strict order may need additional logic.
- Message Size Limit: Standard and FIFO queues both have a maximum message size of 256 KB. Larger messages require alternative handling, such as storing content in S3 and sending a reference.
- Message Retention: Messages are retained for up to 14 days. Longer retention periods require custom solutions.
- Long Polling Duration: Long polling is limited to a maximum wait time of 20 seconds. Longer intervals necessitate alternative approaches.
- Latency: SQS may exhibit higher latency compared to some other messaging systems. Applications requiring ultra-low latency should evaluate other options.
- Operational Overhead: Despite automated infrastructure management, developers must still manage queue configurations, monitoring, and operational settings.
- FIFO Complexity: FIFO queues introduce constraints such as message deduplication and strict ordering, which can complicate application design.
- API Rate Limits: SQS enforces rate limits on API calls, which can affect performance and scalability if not properly managed.
- Data Transfer Costs: Depending on usage patterns, data transfer fees between SQS and other AWS services or external systems may apply.

Common Use Cases for AWS SQS:
1. Scalable Message Processing: SQS enables the construction of highly available, scalable systems for message handling. It decouples application components, allowing them to operate independently and at varying speeds. This is ideal for high-volume scenarios, with the ability to process millions of messages per second, ensuring seamless scaling under increased load.
2. Asynchronous Communication: SQS is widely used for asynchronous communication between microservices. Services can exchange messages via queues without direct integration, improving system resilience and flexibility. Each service processes messages at its own pace, enhancing overall reliability.
3. Event-Driven Architecture: SQS supports event-driven designs where components respond to events published to queues. Multiple subscribers can process events asynchronously, promoting loose coupling and enabling easy scaling and fault tolerance—especially valuable for real-time processing needs.
4. Delayed Message Processing: SQS allows messages to be delayed before becoming available for processing. This capability supports time-sensitive operations, scheduled tasks, and retry mechanisms with exponential backoff.
5. Fault Tolerance and Redundancy: By replicating messages across multiple availability zones, SQS ensures high availability and fault tolerance. It automatically scales to meet demand, making it resilient to traffic spikes and infrastructure failures.
6. Batch Processing: SQS supports sending and receiving multiple messages in a single API call, reducing overhead and latency. This improves efficiency, especially when handling large message volumes by minimizing the number of requests.
7. Dead Letter Queues: SQS provides Dead Letter Queues (DLQs) to manage messages that fail processing after repeated attempts. Failed messages are automatically moved to a DLQ for inspection or manual handling, helping prevent message loss and supporting error diagnosis.
8. Fanout Pattern: SQS can serve as a scalable publish-subscribe mechanism. A single message can be published to a topic, with multiple queues subscribing to receive it. This enables efficient broadcasting to multiple consumers, decoupling publishers from subscribers.

Regarding developer roles, the following outlines typical responsibilities and experience levels:

Junior Developer: Typically has 0–2 years of experience. Focuses on learning core technologies, writing basic code, and supporting team tasks under supervision. Responsibilities include bug fixing, simple feature implementation, and following established coding standards.

Middle Developer: Has 2–5 years of experience. Takes ownership of specific modules or features, contributes to design discussions, and writes clean, maintainable code. Responsibilities include debugging complex issues, collaborating with peers, and participating in code reviews.

Senior Developer: Has 5–8 years of experience. Leads technical decisions, mentors junior developers, and designs scalable system components. Responsibilities include architecture planning, performance optimization, and ensuring code quality and security across projects.

Expert/Team Lead: Has 8+ years of experience. Guides overall technical direction, manages teams, and aligns development with business goals. Responsibilities include strategic planning, cross-team coordination, advanced problem solving, and driving innovation within the engineering organization. Average annual salaries vary by region and company but reflect these experience and responsibility levels.

Zero-waste eSourcing: strategies for sustainable material procurement  
Updated: Apr 8  

The idea of adopting zero-waste practices often leads to the misconception that it requires significant investment with little return. However, this is far from accurate. At its heart, zero-waste eSourcing is a strategic procurement approach designed to prevent waste from occurring in the first place. In light of increasing environmental pressures and rising expectations for corporate responsibility, sustainable material procurement is no longer just an ethical choice—it is a critical business strategy.

This article explores the concept of zero-waste eSourcing, highlighting its importance and offering practical strategies and best practices to integrate zero-waste principles into digital procurement processes.

1. Understanding zero-waste eSourcing  
Zero-waste eSourcing involves rethinking procurement to align with environmental sustainability. It emphasizes sourcing materials in a way that generates no waste, significantly reducing environmental harm. This approach prioritizes resource efficiency and supports the circular economy by extending the lifecycle of materials as much as possible. With the European Union setting ambitious targets—requiring most sectors to cut total waste by 50 to 60% by 2030—zero-waste procurement has evolved from an environmental aspiration into a comprehensive business strategy that improves resource utilization and strengthens long-term sustainability.

2. Setting sustainable material procurement goals  
Effective zero-waste eSourcing begins with well-defined, measurable objectives. Organizations must clearly articulate what success looks like in terms of waste reduction, resource conservation, and environmental responsibility. Establishing baseline metrics and using structured frameworks such as the Science Based Targets initiative helps companies map their sustainability journey. Understanding the three scopes of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions provides deeper insight into the environmental impact of procurement decisions, reinforcing the need for a strategic, holistic approach to lowering a company’s carbon footprint.

A key element of sustainable procurement is managing GHG emissions across the entire supply chain. Scope 1 emissions refer to direct emissions from owned or controlled sources. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from the generation of purchased energy. Scope 3 includes all other indirect emissions occurring across a company’s value chain—upstream and downstream—such as those from raw material extraction, transportation, and product use. Although Scope 1 and 2 emissions are more directly controllable, Scope 3 emissions typically represent the largest portion of a company’s carbon footprint. Addressing them demands a sophisticated strategy involving supplier collaboration, data transparency, and proactive sourcing decisions.

3. Financial and regulatory drivers  
Sustainable procurement delivers tangible financial benefits. By optimizing resource use and reducing waste, companies can lower operational costs and improve profitability. Additionally, building resilience against economic volatility and regulatory shifts—such as trade restrictions or carbon pricing—enhances long-term business stability.

Shifting perspective is essential: sustainability should not be seen as a cost burden but as a strategic investment. While sustainable sourcing may involve higher initial expenses, it can lead to long-term savings, operational improvements, innovation, and stronger market positioning. These advantages make sustainability a driver of competitive advantage rather than a financial drain.

4. Leveraging eSourcing platforms for sustainability  
In today’s digital landscape, technology plays a vital role in advancing sustainability. eSourcing platforms provide powerful tools that support zero-waste objectives by enabling supplier transparency, conducting life cycle assessments, and assigning sustainability ratings. These capabilities streamline procurement while embedding environmental and social criteria into supplier selection and management.

Platforms like Valcori offer built-in scoring systems within the RFx (request for quote, proposal, or information) process, allowing organizations to assign different weights to various ESG (environmental, social, and governance) criteria. This customization makes it easier and faster to identify suppliers that meet sustainability standards, ensuring that sustainability is not an afterthought but a core evaluation factor.

Furthermore, sustainable procurement helps mitigate risks tied to unethical practices such as labor violations or environmental damage. By assessing suppliers based on their sustainability commitments, companies ensure ethical sourcing, protect their brand reputation, and reduce exposure to legal and reputational risks.

5. Promoting innovation and continuous improvement  
Achieving zero-waste goals requires ongoing innovation. The pursuit of sustainability often reveals opportunities for cost reduction, process optimization, and efficiency gains across the supply chain. Benefits of sustainable procurement include lower total cost of ownership, improved regulatory compliance, and stronger brand credibility.

To sustain progress, organizations must implement feedback loops and performance tracking systems. This ensures that zero-waste efforts are not one-off projects but part of a continuous improvement cycle. Sustainability becomes embedded in the procurement culture, driving long-term transformation.

Zero-waste eSourcing is not a passing trend—it is a fundamental strategy for businesses aiming to succeed in an era defined by environmental awareness and stakeholder expectations. By adopting the practices discussed, companies can reduce their ecological footprint, demonstrate corporate responsibility, and contribute to a more sustainable future. As this discussion concludes, we encourage organizations to act now—integrate zero-waste principles into their eSourcing processes, and join the global movement toward sustainability. Let’s work together, share insights, and drive innovation on this essential journey.

In-hospital falls following anesthesia can lead to serious clinical complications, yet the role of anesthesia in triggering such events remains unclear. Anesthesia may contribute to postoperative falls due to lingering pharmacologic effects and neuromuscular blockade from anesthetic agents. This study retrospectively analyzed in-hospital falls occurring within 24 hours after anesthesia at Hualien Buddhist Tzu Chi General Hospital between January 2009 and December 2013 to determine the incidence and identify associated risk factors.

A total of 60,796 inpatients received anesthesia during the study period, with ten falls recorded within 24 hours post-anesthesia. All falls occurred in general wards, with a higher frequency at the bedside, during periods when caregivers were present, and during daytime hours. Older age and the use of regional anesthesia were significant independent risk factors for postanesthesia falls, while gender and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status did not show a significant association. The overall incidence proportion of postanesthesia falls was 1.6 per 10,000 patients (95% CI 0.006% to 0.026%) over the 24-hour observation window. Falls were more likely to occur during less anticipated postoperative periods and were more common among elderly patients and those receiving regional anesthesia.

Postoperative falls are a relatively rare but clinically significant complication that can result in fractures, traumatic head injuries, visceral contusions, and skin abrasions. These events not only extend hospital stays and increase medical costs but may also lead to avoidable medical disputes. Despite their potential severity, falls during the postoperative phase have been under-investigated. Previous studies report postoperative fall rates of 1.6% to 1.8% in veteran medical centers, with an average time to fall of 12 days post-surgery. The theoretical risk of increased falls after anesthesia due to residual drug effects has not been clearly established in prior research, and no study has specifically reported the incidence of falls immediately after anesthesia. This study fills that gap by analyzing postanesthesia records from 2009 to 2013 to characterize fall events and identify risk factors, with the long-term goal of informing targeted prevention strategies for high-risk surgical patients.

The study was a retrospective chart review approved by the hospital’s ethics committee and institutional review board (IRB approval number IRB103-14-B), with written informed consent waived. The hospital is a tertiary teaching center with 945 beds in Hualien City, Taiwan. Postoperative bedside visits by nurse anesthetists were conducted for all inpatients who received anesthesia for surgery or other invasive procedures. These visits documented pain scores, patient satisfaction, and anesthesia-related complications. Ward nurses recorded all postoperative adverse events, including falls, defined as sudden, unintended descents to the floor or lower surfaces. Medical records of patients who fell within 24 hours of anesthesia were reviewed by staff anesthesiologists to assess fall characteristics. Patients who received only local infiltration anesthesia and were discharged within 24 hours of anesthesia were excluded.

The incidence proportion of postanesthesia falls was calculated as the number of falls divided by the total number of inpatient surgical cases receiving anesthesia. Potential risk factors included age groups, gender, ASA physical status, and type of anesthesia. A Poisson regression model was used to analyze associations between these factors and fall occurrence. The model fit the data well, as indicated by a non-significant goodness-of-fit chi-squared test (p = 0.995). Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. All analyses were conducted using SAS 9.4 software.

From January 2009 to December 2013, 78,064 patients received anesthesia for surgical or invasive procedures. Of these, 60,796 (77.9%) were hospitalized for at least 24 hours post-anesthesia. Patient demographics and surgical procedures are summarized in Table 1. The overall post-anesthesia visit completion rate was 98.7 ± 0.5% over the five years, with less than 0.5% missing data in the electronic database.

Ten falls occurred within 24 hours of anesthesia, resulting in an incidence proportion of 0.016% (95% CI 0.006% to 0.026%). The average time to fall was 13.3 ± 8.4 hours (range 2.6–24 hours). All falls occurred in general wards, with no incidents reported in special care units. Most falls were minor and did not prolong hospitalization, though three patients sustained more severe injuries requiring additional medical or surgical intervention (Table 2).

Risk factor analysis showed no significant differences in gender or ASA physical status between fall patients and the overall cohort (Tables 4 and 5). However, older age and the type of anesthesia were significant and independent predictors of postanesthesia falls. Patients aged 40–70 years (mean age 65 ± 15 years) had a significantly higher incidence of falls compared to younger patients (P < 0.001). Similarly, patients receiving regional anesthesia (neuroaxial blocks) and intravenous sedation anesthesia had significantly higher fall rates (P < 0.001 and P = 0.002, respectively).

The Biological Evolution of Pain  
by Socrethics First version 2007 Last version 2018  

The capacity to experience pain increases with evolutionary development and appears to have no inherent limit. Similarly, the ability to feel pleasure also evolves, but the presence of pain cannot be offset by pleasure when comparing individuals.  

Key questions addressed include:  
- What role does pain play in evolution?  
- Why does pain increase over time?  
- How does the distribution of pain change across species and populations?  

Pain is fundamentally linked to harmful or potentially damaging stimuli, a connection shaped by natural selection. In many cases, pain functions as an adaptive trait that enhances survival and reproductive success. However, pain can also arise as a non-adaptive by-product of genetic variation. The same allele may lead to either maladaptive suffering or beneficial adaptation depending on interactions with other genes. If the overall effect is a net increase in biological fitness, the allele is likely to become more common in the population.  

The rise in pain sensitivity correlates with the growing importance of learning mechanisms. As organisms live longer and face more complex environments, their behavior becomes increasingly shaped by past painful experiences. A broad range of emotions enhances adaptive responses to environmental challenges. This emotional complexity involves intense and prolonged pain states, which, under these conditions, contribute to greater fitness.  

Regarding the distribution of pain, biological altruism can reduce or mitigate pain in some cases. Nevertheless, a general trend points toward increasing inequality in pain distribution. Whether this evolutionary pattern continues at the cultural level remains an open question.  

Pain is defined as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience tied to actual or potential tissue damage, as established by the International Association for the Study of Pain. It functions as part of the body’s defense system, triggering reflexive withdrawal from harmful stimuli, protective behaviors during healing, and avoidance of future danger. While suffering encompasses various negative states like hunger or sexual deprivation, pain is typically restricted to experiences involving physical damage or threat to bodily integrity. Research focuses on pain as a priority, though the ultimate aim is understanding the evolution of suffering.  

Conditions for pain to exist include:  
1. Conscious experience — only conscious beings can undergo pain.  
2. A phenomenal self-model — pain involves a core sense of ownership, the subjective awareness that the experience is happening to oneself.  
3. Negative valence — pain arises when negative value is integrated into the self-model. This does not require full cognitive understanding; it suffices that the organism avoids or seeks to end the experience. Even the expectation of negative outcomes can generate a strong urge for change.  
4. Phenomenal transparency — conscious states appear directly and irrevocably real, without awareness of the underlying mental medium. This creates a subjective sense of immediacy and certainty.  

In human pain assessment, self-reporting remains the primary method, such as rating pain on a scale from none to extreme. However, reliability is limited by potential deception or self-misinterpretation. Recent advances in neuroimaging, particularly MRI analysis, offer new ways to detect pain from external measurements, reigniting debate over whether pain can be objectively quantified.  

Behavioral assessment reveals that pain is often intensely expressed — a minor injury may cause prolonged distress, vocalization, and immobilization. Yet such responses can attract predators, raising the evolutionary puzzle of why pain remains so intense. The interpretation of pain-related behaviors depends on understanding the species’ ecological and social context. Vocalization of pain can be adaptive in social species where others may assist in defense, such as in humans, primates, dogs, and pigs. In solitary species where cooperation is rare, vocalizing may attract predators and thus be disadvantageous, as seen in antelopes and sheep. If vocalization provides a net reproductive benefit, it will spread in the population; otherwise, it will not.  

Anatomical and physiological assessment distinguishes between nociception — the detection of harmful stimuli — and pain, which includes an emotional dimension. The International Association for the Study of Pain emphasizes that nociceptor activation alone does not constitute pain. While peripheral structures and basic physiological mechanisms of pain are largely conserved across vertebrates, functional roles of brain regions differ significantly between groups. It is therefore illogical to conclude that a function is absent in a species simply because a particular brain region is small or missing. Pain perception can occur without direct involvement of nociceptors, just as vision or hearing can occur without their sensory receptors. Thus, the pain system must be evaluated as an integrated whole.  

A holistic approach to assessing pain includes:  
- Brain structures involved in pain processing  
- Neural pathways leading to higher brain centers  
- Presence and function of opioid receptors and endogenous pain-relieving substances  
- Reduction of pain responses through analgesics  
- Evidence of avoidance learning  
- Disruption of normal behavior during pain  

Regarding fish, several conflicting views exist. Some claim fish cannot experience pain, fear, or emotions (Rose 2002). Others argue that a proper assessment requires detailed knowledge of forebrain neuroanatomy and how it mediates behavior (Chandroo 2004). Electrophysiological studies show fish nociceptors are nearly identical to those in higher vertebrates, suggesting these traits evolved prior to the divergence of fish lineages (Sneddon 2004). More recent research challenges the idea that fish lack pain perception, with evidence supporting conscious awareness of pain (Braithwaite 2010). Studies increasingly question the long-held assumption that fish cannot feel pain (Segner 2012). In contrast, mammals, birds, and reptiles exhibit clear emotional responses, while fish and amphibians do not. Higher vertebrates also possess more dopamine receptors, which are strongly linked to reward systems (Holmes 2017).  

For invertebrates, the evidence is mixed. Some sources suggest most invertebrates, especially insects, do not experience pain (Senate of Canada 2003), while others indicate that certain invertebrates may be capable of pain (Braithwaite 2010, Stelling 2014). It is nearly certain that simple organisms like amoebas lack sentience (DeGrazia 2002).

A blocked drain can range from a minor annoyance to a serious issue that jeopardizes your home’s structural integrity, potentially costing between £100 and £900 to resolve depending on the underlying cause. Understanding how to respond effectively can help reduce damage and lead to a quicker, more sustainable fix. This guide outlines key steps and considerations for addressing a blocked drain in London.

Blockages can arise from several factors. Structural damage to drainage pipes may restrict flow, while physical obstructions such as debris or foreign objects can become lodged within the system. Older pipes often lose efficiency over time, leading to sluggish drainage and eventual blockages. Ground movement, especially in areas with shifting soil, can misalign or crush pipes, disrupting drainage. In regions with hard water, mineral deposits can accumulate inside pipes, gradually narrowing the passage and contributing to blockages.

Common warning signs include water draining more slowly than usual, flooding on the property, wastewater flowing back into sinks or toilets, persistent foul odours emanating from drains, and gurgling noises within the drainage system—indicative of air trapped due to partial or complete blockages.

For internal blockages, a plunger can be an effective and affordable solution, typically costing as little as £6. It works well on toilets, sinks, and plugholes. Drain unblockers available over the counter can also assist by dissolving organic materials like soap scum, grease, and grime that contribute to clogs. However, these should be used cautiously, following instructions to avoid pipe damage.

When the blockage lies outside your property boundary—such as in public sewers or shared drainage systems—it’s important to determine responsibility before taking action. In many cases, the local sewerage company is responsible for these sections. If the source of the blockage is unclear, attempting to resolve it without proper diagnosis may lead to ineffective or unsafe outcomes.

Engaging a professional plumber is often the most reliable course of action, particularly for complex or recurring issues. Plumbers possess the expertise and specialized tools needed to diagnose and resolve drainage problems. Upon arrival, they typically conduct a thorough assessment and may employ one or more of the following methods: applying chemical treatments to break down organic matter, using high-pressure jet washers to clear severe blockages, deploying drain augers (also known as plumbing snakes) to physically remove obstructions, or inserting a drain camera to inspect the interior of pipes and pinpoint the exact location and nature of the issue.

While hiring professionals involves a cost, it offers long-term benefits. Temporary fixes may mask symptoms but fail to address the root cause, potentially allowing water to accumulate and lead to structural damage, mold growth, or further deterioration. By identifying and resolving the underlying problem, professional intervention prevents future complications and avoids more extensive and expensive repairs down the line.

The Boomerang Nebula, a proto-planetary nebula formed by a dying red giant star approximately 5000 light years from Earth, has puzzled astronomers since its discovery in 1980 by a team using the Anglo-Australian telescope at Siding Spring Observatory. Its mystery intensified in 1995 when observations with the now-decommissioned 15-meter Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) in Chile revealed it to be the coldest known object in the Universe. Recent research using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in northern Chile now offers a compelling explanation: the nebula’s extreme cold likely results from a binary interaction involving a small companion star plunging into the red giant.

The findings, detailed in a paper titled “The Coldest Place in the Universe: Probing the Ultra-cold Outflow and Dusty Disk in the Boomerang Nebula” published in the Astrophysical Journal, are led by Raghvendra Sahai of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. According to the study, the rapid expansion of gas ejected from the central star—driven by a powerful jet—cools the material to temperatures below the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), the residual radiation from the Big Bang that sets the baseline temperature of space at 2.725 K (–270.4 °C; –454.7 °F). The Boomerang Nebula’s temperature is less than half a Kelvin, or –272.5 °C (–458.5 °F), making it colder than the CMB.

This extreme cooling is attributed to a gas cloud extending up to 21,000 astronomical units (AU) from the central star, with outflows reaching distances of 120,000 AU. ALMA’s high-resolution observations revealed previously unseen structures in the outflow, showing expansion speeds about ten times faster than what a single red giant could achieve. The team concludes this extraordinary ejection of mass and energy must have been powered by gravitational interactions between two stars.

They propose that the red giant, which was in the Red Giant Branch (RGB) or early-RGB phase of its evolution, had a binary companion that was drawn in by its expanding gravity. The companion eventually merged with the core of the red giant, triggering a violent outflow of material. Sahai emphasized in a NRAO press release that the sheer mass and velocity of the ejected gas could only be explained by the energy released from such a binary interaction: “These new data show us that most of the stellar envelope from the massive red giant star has been blasted out into space at speeds far beyond the capabilities of a single, red giant star. The only way to eject so much mass and at such extreme speeds is from the gravitational energy of two interacting stars, which would explain the puzzling properties of the ultra-cold outflow.”

ALMA’s precision enabled the team to estimate the outflow’s age at between 1050 and 1925 years, and to measure its mass and kinetic energy. However, the nebula’s current status as the coldest known object may not last. The central star is expected to evolve further into a planetary nebula, shedding more material and gradually shrinking and heating up. As it does, the surrounding nebula will warm and brighten, ending its period of extreme cold.

Lars-Åke Nyman, an astronomer at the Joint ALMA Observatory in Santiago, Chile, and a co-author of the study, noted that the Boomerang Nebula represents a fleeting phase in stellar evolution: “We see this remarkable object at a very special, very short-lived period of its life. It’s possible these super cosmic freezers are quite common in the universe, but they can only maintain such extreme temperatures for a relatively short time.”

These findings also shed light on broader astrophysical processes, particularly the behavior of binary systems involving massive stars. When a red giant expands and engulfs its companion, such interactions can produce ultra-cold outflows, potentially creating similar “cosmic freezers” elsewhere. The Boomerang Nebula thus challenges traditional models of stellar evolution and binary dynamics.

Moreover, the study highlights the transformative power of next-generation instruments like ALMA. With their exceptional resolution and sensitivity, such observatories allow astronomers to observe phenomena never before seen, continually expanding our understanding of the cosmos and prompting reevaluation of what is physically possible in the universe.

The intensity of earthquake ground motion is typically assessed using peak ground acceleration and spectral acceleration, which are strength-based or force-based measures. Contemporary seismic design codes employ strength-based methodologies, representing seismic demand through elastic response spectra. These approaches incorporate a structure's ductility through reduction factors, but they do not directly account for the cyclic nature of structural response or the accumulation of damage over time. In contrast, energy-based parameters can be formulated to capture both the amplitude of shaking and the number of cycles experienced, making them potentially more effective in correlating with actual structural damage. This study evaluates the relationship between structural damage and both strength- and energy-based parameters through inelastic dynamic analyses of reinforced concrete and steel buildings. The 1999 earthquakes in Turkey, along with the observed structural damage, provide a regional context for analyzing recorded ground motions across varying distances and for structures with different natural periods. This regional framework, centered on northwestern Turkey, is also applied in probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA), where design ground motions for different return periods—derived from both strength and energy perspectives—are compared across four specific sites and across broader maps covering the Istanbul region. New attenuation models for both strength- and energy-based parameters are developed using a comprehensive dataset of earthquakes in Turkey. A key feature of these models is their use of random effects models that distinguish between inter-event variability (differences between earthquakes) and intra-event variability (differences within a single earthquake). These models reveal variations in strength and energy demands across different locations. When hazard results from the new Turkish models are compared with those from models used in the western United States, differences in design motions based on strength are notable, but the differences are smaller when energy-based considerations are used.

Leaving a pet in a parked vehicle on a warm day can quickly lead to heatstroke or suffocation, even if the outside temperature is mild. On a seemingly pleasant 78-degree day, the interior of a car parked in the shade can rise above 90 degrees, and temperatures can soar to 160 degrees when exposed to direct sunlight. This risk persists even when temperatures are in the 60s, as sunlight can rapidly elevate the internal temperature of a vehicle to dangerous levels. Experts strongly advise against leaving pets or children unattended in cars for any length of time when the temperature is 60 degrees or higher, regardless of whether windows are cracked or the car is in the shade. While opening a window may offer minimal relief, it does not ensure safety and can allow the pet to escape. Additionally, if someone attempts to assist a pet through a window and is bitten, the owner may be held legally responsible.

Relying on air conditioning to keep a pet safe in a car is also risky. Mechanical failures can occur, such as the air conditioning compressor shutting down due to engine overheating, even in modern vehicles with advanced systems. In 2003, a police dog in Texas died after the air conditioning in a patrol car stopped working and began circulating hot air. Similarly, in August 2004, a North Carolina couple lost two dogs and nearly lost a third after their car’s air conditioning failed during a shopping trip lasting less than 30 minutes, despite having provided water and ice. These incidents highlight that no system is foolproof.

Animals, particularly dogs, cannot sweat like humans do. They regulate body temperature primarily through panting and limited sweat glands on their paw pads. When forced to breathe hot air, they are at high risk of overheating, which can lead to collapse, brain damage, or death. In as little as 15 minutes, a dog’s body temperature can rise from a normal 102.5°F to life-threatening levels, causing irreversible damage to the nervous and cardiovascular systems. Symptoms of heat exhaustion include restlessness, extreme thirst, heavy panting, lethargy, a dark tongue, rapid pulse, fever, vomiting, glazed eyes, dizziness, and loss of coordination. If these signs are observed, immediate action is required: provide fresh water, apply a cold towel or ice pack to the head, neck, and chest, and gradually cool the dog in cool (not icy) water. Seek veterinary care promptly.

Preventive measures include leaving pets at home on warm days, bringing ample fresh water and a bowl on trips, and never allowing dogs to ride loose in pickup truck beds. Hot metal surfaces can burn paws, sunlight and debris pose injury risks, sudden braking may cause a fall, and the dog may jump out if startled or excited. Using a crate to secure the dog in a safer space is recommended when the animal cannot ride inside the cab.

If a pet is seen in a hot car, take immediate steps: record the vehicle’s make, model, color, and license plate number, then go to the nearest business and ask staff to page the owner. Contact local police, who typically respond faster than animal control and have the authority to enter the vehicle and rescue the animal. In most areas, it is illegal to leave a pet unattended in a parked or standing vehicle if it endangers the animal’s health or safety.

Maryland’s legal code, under the Cruelty to Animals section, states that no person may leave a cat or dog unattended in a parked or standing vehicle in a way that endangers the animal. Authorized individuals—including law enforcement officers, public safety employees, animal control officers, officers from state-authorized animal welfare organizations, and fire and rescue personnel—may use reasonable force to remove an animal from a vehicle in violation of this rule. These individuals are protected from liability for damages resulting from such actions.

Educational resources are available to help raise awareness. The Humane Society of the United States offers free flyers and posters that can be distributed to stores to remind the public that leaving a pet in a parked car can be fatal. These materials can be obtained by calling 202-452-1100 or emailing firstname.lastname@example.com. Additionally, brief leaflets on topics like pets in hot cars and chaining dogs can be downloaded online. A Hot Dog car sunshade with an educational message is available through PETA by calling 1-800-483-4366.

For those interested in promoting public awareness, the organization offers a Public Service Announcement about the dangers of leaving pets in hot cars, which can be requested by contacting 757-622-7382. Additional resources on pet safety, including a Summer Pet Safety Guide, Poison Emergency 24-Hour Hotlines, and tips on keeping dogs cool in hot weather, are available through the Partnership for Animal Welfare. The information was last updated on June 18, 2015.
