When a baby arrives, parents expect sleepless nights and frequent feedings. However, caring for a high need infant brings a different challenge—one marked by extended periods of wakefulness and fussiness, with little relief despite consistent soothing efforts. Even when sleep is achieved, the baby may be so deeply asleep that moving them becomes impossible, making crib placement difficult. If you're reading this, your child likely has a more intense temperament than others, and you're probably feeling drained.

As a children’s sleep specialist working with families of children under six, I help parents guide their children toward better sleep habits—including overnight sleep—without resorting to cry-it-out methods. I’m also a mother to a high need child; my eldest daughter, now nearly eight, has always been more intense and demanding than her peers and required significant support to learn how to fall asleep independently. Most of the families I work with have high need children, and research supports that more intense children typically need more assistance developing independent sleep skills. In contrast, easygoing babies who fall asleep anywhere are uncommon in my practice.

To help ease the sleep struggle, consider these strategies. Consistent routines are vital, especially for high need children who thrive on predictability. A daily schedule helps prevent overtiredness by keeping naps and meals at fixed times, avoiding hunger-related nap disruptions. When a child shows early signs of fatigue—such as yawning, ear pulling, or increased noise—they are likely already at their sleep window. By the time caregivers finish preparations, the child may be overtired, making sleep harder to initiate and maintain.

Establishing predictable nap and nighttime routines can support relaxation. A 10 to 15 minute nap routine and a 30-minute to one-hour bedtime routine are ideal. Consistency is key—perform the same steps in the same order and location each time. Over time, the routine itself becomes a signal for calm and sleep.

If your child is overstimulated before a nap—evidenced by short naps of 20 to 30 minutes—introduce a walking wind down. About 10 to 15 minutes before the nap routine, take your child away from toys and go for a quiet walk. Look out windows, sing softly, and help them unwind. This allows their brain to slow down, increasing the likelihood of falling asleep and staying asleep longer.

To enhance comfort and familiarity, use a crib sheet and swaddling blanket that have been worn close to your body so they carry your scent. Place the scented sheet on the mattress before putting your child down, and swaddle them in the familiar blanket. I recommend swaddling all high need infants until they can roll over independently. Ensure the crib is not cold—transitioning from a warm, held position to a cool crib can wake a baby. To warm the mattress safely, place a heating pad under the sheet, remove it before placing your child in the crib, and confirm the mattress isn’t too hot. Stay with your child for at least 20 minutes after they fall asleep to support deep sleep and reduce the need for repeated interventions.

Around six months, encourage self-soothing with the pacifier. Instead of placing it in your child’s mouth, give it to their hand and gently guide it if needed. This teaches them to reinsert the pacifier independently. Play a game called “hide the paci” when your child is alert and not hungry. Hide several pacifiers under a toy or blanket and praise your child when they find one. This reinforces the idea that pacifiers are available in the crib even when unseen. Place at least half a dozen pacifiers in the crib at each sleep time to increase the chance of your child finding one during the night. If your child sleeps with clenched fists, place a pacifier in each hand after they are asleep so they don’t need to search.

While these techniques may not guarantee overnight sleep, they can make sleep more attainable and less stressful. For parents of high need, fussy infants, every additional minute of rest counts. Rebecca Michi is a parenting consultant and children’s sleep specialist based in the Seattle area. For more information about her services, visit her website.

For families dealing with early morning wake-ups in toddlers or preschoolers, the Zazoo photo clock can help. This multimedia clock shows a bright, cheerful sun scene at wake-up time and a moon at bedtime, supporting healthy sleep habits in children who can’t yet read traditional clocks.

Additional resources include: Stop Crying, Calm Down, and Other Things We Tell Our High Need Kids, BS Facts About Baby Sleep That Everyone Thinks Are True, Holly’s Top 3 Tips for Getting Your Child to Sleep, 5 Common Childhood Sleep Myths Debunked, Transitioning to One Nap – Winning the Dreaded Nap Battle, and Sleep Strategies for Babies 101.

Structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a valuable tool for visualizing the internal architecture of the brain. It is extensively employed in detecting brain tumors due to its ability to produce high-resolution images of soft brain tissues. Identifying and classifying brain tumors is a crucial yet time-intensive process typically carried out by radiologists. Tumors can vary significantly in size, shape, and location, and accurately extracting the tumor region while detecting subtle differences remains challenging for human experts. Digital image processing techniques—such as preprocessing, segmentation, and classification—play a vital role in assisting clinical professionals with precise brain tumor diagnosis. This paper reviews recent advancements in brain tumor detection using MRI images, providing an in-depth analysis of cutting-edge machine learning and deep learning approaches. It also examines available datasets and highlights existing challenges in the field. The comprehensive survey aims to support future research efforts in developing improved decision support systems, ultimately aiding radiologists in achieving more accurate and reliable brain tumor diagnoses.

When a peer reviewer, after carefully studying a scientific paper, feels confident they can fully grasp both the methodology and rationale behind the research, and could realistically reproduce the findings in their own lab with a reasonable chance of success, the paper is considered sufficiently transparent. However, this ideal is rarely achieved in practice. Paradoxically, the more comprehensive a paper is, the less incentive readers have to attempt replication. Nevertheless, the fundamental principle stands: for a scientific paper to be credible, it must contain the essential elements required for replication. This principle is widely accepted across the scientific community.

It is therefore noteworthy that the situation has reversed in a striking way—an apparent lack of clear rules is now being invoked to obstruct scientific communication. Who supports such a restrictive and narrow interpretation of data access? 

While historical context is important, the current relevance lies in how this issue is perceived today, particularly in relation to Nature and the Jones et al. 1990 paper. On this point, who endorses the earlier interpretation? 

Phil Jones, the lead author of the 1990 paper, does not. He had previously faced requests for the underlying data but never claimed that his paper was exempt from data sharing due to a data policy at Nature. He also did not argue that, because Nature had no formal data policy at the time of publication, he was under no obligation to share. 

His institution, the University of East Anglia (UEA), also did not take that stance. When Steve McIntyre submitted a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, the Climatic Research Unit (CRU) eventually released the Chinese temperature data to him and the public. Fortunately, the data was provided in digital binary format, not on outdated paper tape, which facilitated its use.

Nature magazine itself does not uphold the narrow view. In 2008, when questioned about a materials-related complaint concerning the same Jones et al. 1990 paper, Nature stated it would apply its current editorial standards to prior publications—including those from 1990—if the paper remained scientifically relevant and had not been superseded. This demonstrates that the journal does not treat past publications as bound solely by the data policies that may have existed at the time of publication. Nature made no formal exceptions or cited any official justification for exemption. Thus, the very journal whose author guidelines were misinterpreted as a binding policy does not itself adhere to that restrictive interpretation.

This raises a critical question: why assume that only sequence and crystallography data were required to be made publicly available under Nature’s guidelines? The only plausible explanation is that such a narrow reading was deliberately used to justify exempting Jones from sharing data under imagined or fabricated conditions. Moreover, there persists a belief among some in the climate science community that data from the Chinese station network is solely under Jones’s personal control, allowing him to decide whether and to whom to release it, free from scientific norms. This view, if widespread, must be corrected. The three independent inquiries into the CRU’s scientific practices all reached a unanimous conclusion.

Will further narrow and petty justifications be introduced? Such defenses are strategically deployed to deepen divisions between amateur researchers, skeptical observers, and professional climate scientists. To maintain scientific integrity and trust, it is essential to support climate scientists in resisting these tactics and to ensure that data sharing is treated as a core component of scientific responsibility.

Infants with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are a distinct patient group requiring specialized treatment approaches. Intensive chemotherapy regimens for these infants commonly include postinduction intensification phases with high-dose cytarabine and methotrexate. Despite these aggressive strategies, long-term event-free survival (EFS) rates remain below 50%. Infants diagnosed with congenital leukemia within the first month of life have particularly poor outcomes, with a 17% overall survival (OS). Among infants with MLL gene rearrangements, EFS rates range from 17% to 40%. Poor prognostic factors in this subgroup include specific MLL translocation variants and other molecular features. These infants are typically treated with intensified chemotherapy regimens that include agents not standard in frontline therapy for older children with ALL. However, even with such intensified treatment, outcomes remain suboptimal. The role of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) during first remission for infants with MLL rearrangements remains debated and not clearly established. Similarly, the optimal treatment strategy for infants without MLL translocations is still uncertain.

Adolescents and young adults with ALL have long been recognized as a high-risk population, with outcomes consistently inferior to those of children under 10 years. This disparity is attributed to a higher frequency of adverse prognostic factors at diagnosis, such as elevated white blood cell counts, specific genetic abnormalities, and delayed diagnosis. In addition, this age group experiences higher rates of treatment-related mortality and non-adherence to therapy. Early studies from the United States and France first highlighted the benefit of pediatric treatment regimens over adult-oriented approaches in this population. Subsequent research has confirmed that older adolescents and young adults achieve better outcomes when treated with pediatric-style regimens rather than adult protocols. These findings are supported by evidence from multiple trials, including FRALLE 93, NOPHO 92, MRC ALL, and UKALL XII, which demonstrate improved OS rates with pediatric regimens. The superior outcomes observed with pediatric regimens are not fully understood, but potential explanations may involve differences in treatment intensity, pharmacokinetics, or tolerance to therapy. Given the favorable results achievable with high-risk pediatric ALL chemotherapy, routine use of allogeneic HSCT in first remission is not recommended for adolescents and young adults with ALL.

Adolescents with ALL are at increased risk for therapy-related complications compared to younger children, including osteonecrosis, deep venous thrombosis, and pancreatitis. Osteonecrosis, which was uncommon before the introduction of postinduction intensification, has become more prevalent with improved survival outcomes in patients aged 10 and older. It affects weight-bearing joints in 95% of cases, and over 40% of patients require surgical intervention due to persistent symptoms or mobility limitations. Most cases are diagnosed within the first two years of treatment, often during the maintenance phase.

A three-arm clinical trial is available for eligible patients to evaluate the efficacy of different consolidation and late intensification regimens: clofarabine/etoposide/cyclophosphamide versus cyclophosphamide/etoposide versus the standard cyclophosphamide/thioguanine/cytarabine combination.

Philadelphia chromosome–positive (Ph+) ALL occurs in approximately 3% of pediatric cases, increases in frequency during adolescence, and accounts for 15% to 25% of adult cases. Historically, this subtype was associated with poor prognosis. In 2000, an international pediatric group reported a 7-year EFS of 25% and OS of 36% in Ph+ ALL patients treated without tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). By 2010, the same group reported improved 7-year EFS of 31% and OS of 44% under the same conditions, indicating modest gains with chemotherapy alone. Treatment has evolved from reliance on aggressive chemotherapy and allogeneic HSCT to the current standard of combination therapy using chemotherapy and TKIs.

Before the availability of imatinib mesylate, HSCT from a matched sibling donor was considered the preferred treatment for Ph+ ALL. Retrospective analyses have shown that matched sibling donor transplants were associated with better outcomes than standard chemotherapy in children and young adults. In contrast, transplants from unrelated donors yielded poor results in these studies. However, a later follow-up study found that both matched-related and matched-unrelated donor transplants had comparable outcomes in the pre-imatinib era. Disease-free survival at 5 years showed a borderline significant advantage for transplantation over chemotherapy (P = .049), and overall survival was also higher in the transplant group, though not significantly so at the 5-year mark.

In the pre-TKI era, favorable prognostic factors included younger age at diagnosis, lower white blood cell count, and favorable response to initial therapy. Monitoring minimal residual disease (MRD) via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction for the BCR-ABL fusion transcript was also found to be helpful in predicting outcomes.

Imatinib mesylate is a selective inhibitor of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. Phase I and II trials of imatinib as a single agent in relapsed or refractory Ph+ ALL demonstrated high response rates, although responses were often short-lived. Clinical trials in both adults and children have confirmed the feasibility of combining imatinib with multiagent chemotherapy. Preliminary data suggest that outcomes after HSCT are improved when imatinib is administered either before or after transplantation.

Dasatinib, a second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is currently under investigation in the frontline treatment of Ph+ ALL. It has demonstrated significant central nervous system (CNS) activity in both preclinical models and clinical series involving patients with CNS-positive leukemia. A phase I trial in pediatric patients showed that once-daily dosing of dasatinib was associated with a manageable toxicity profile, with few nonhematologic grade 3 or 4 adverse events.

Patients may be eligible to participate in U.S. clinical trials for Philadelphia chromosome-positive childhood precursor ALL. The National Cancer Institute provides a searchable list of active cancer clinical trials that are currently enrolling patients. This list can be refined by location, specific drugs, interventions, and other criteria to identify suitable studies.

From July 3 to 15, Ximena Roncancio from Colombia, Armand Kablam from Côte d'Ivoire, Khalid Bahaudin from Bangladesh, and Antonethe Castaneda from Guatemala—members of the Young Scientists of IRDR—attended the São Paulo School of Advanced Science on Climate Change: Scientific Basis, Adaptation, Vulnerability, and Mitigation. The school was designed to advance the training of graduate students in climate change-related fields, promoting interdisciplinary and intersectoral knowledge exchange among participants, lecturers, and organizers. It also aimed to build collaborative networks that bring together a critical mass of young researchers dedicated to understanding climate change and its impacts on ecosystems and society.

Environmental research inherently involves diverse topics such as water resources, land use, biodiversity, pollution, and food security. Climate change intensifies this complexity, necessitating more comprehensive and interdisciplinary approaches to inform effective decision-making and actions for the benefit of both the planet and human societies. Due to its global significance, climate change has remained a prominent public issue since the establishment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in 1988. In response, numerous countries have launched initiatives to strengthen climate change research. In Brazil, key programs include the FAPESP Research Program on Global Climate Change (RPGCC), the Brazilian Research Network on Global Climate Change (Rede Clima), the Brazilian Panel on Climate Change (PBMC), and the INCT for Climate Change (INCT-MC). Within Brazil’s academic landscape, research groups like INCLINE have played a significant role in advancing climate change science through collaborative efforts involving multiple scientists and universities.

The São Paulo School of Advanced Science provided graduate students with advanced training in climate change science and related topics, including public policy dimensions. Participants engaged in in-depth discussions with leading scientists on central themes from the three working groups of the IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report, within a multidisciplinary and multicultural setting. Young Scientists of IRDR members presented scientific posters, joining postdoctoral researchers, PhD students, and master’s students from various countries. A notable feature of the event was the opportunity for meaningful interaction among participants beyond previous online connections. 

Source: http://www.incline.iag.usp.br/data/spsas_about.php

The crew takes on a fun challenge: what knife would you choose with a budget of $25, $100, or $300? We’re not claiming these selections are the absolute best value, but each was picked for specific, thoughtful reasons. This episode offers some surprising picks and is a lighthearted look at knife preferences. We invite you to share your own choices in our Facebook group, “Mark of the Maker.” In our second Minisode, Tom Krein discusses the Crossada and explores how James Keating’s legendary fighting knife design has shaped his own craftsmanship. These brief minisodes are designed to deepen understanding by highlighting key influences and their impact on a knifemaker’s development and artistic style.

Digital technology is fundamentally reshaping how healthcare professionals communicate and engage with patients. From accessing lab results to managing appointments, information technology systems have advanced rapidly, rendering traditional paper-based processes increasingly obsolete and inefficient. While much of my work centers on guiding IT vendors in navigating the healthcare sector, it’s essential to periodically revisit foundational principles to help hospitals make informed choices about the technologies they adopt. Based on this perspective, here are five critical systems that every hospital should prioritize investing in today.

Speech recognition technology offers a powerful tool for directly entering clinical data into personal health records, whether in outpatient clinics or at the patient’s bedside. This capability significantly boosts productivity, reduces document processing times, and lowers operational costs associated with paper, ink, and manual labor. Given the inefficiencies and high costs of paper-based documentation, integrating speech recognition is a strategic move toward modernizing clinical workflows.

Electronic Document Management (EDM) systems play a vital role in building robust electronic health records (EHR) infrastructures. Hospitals can choose between adopting a single integrated vendor solution or assembling a customized system using specialized components. In either case, an EDM system serves as a vendor-neutral central archive, enabling efficient data storage, retrieval, and secure sharing across departments. Regardless of the overall EHR strategy, incorporating EDM should be a standard consideration in any digital transformation plan.

Clinical portals function as unified dashboards that consolidate and display data from multiple, often fragmented, electronic health record systems across different hospital departments. With many institutions already operating several independent EHR platforms, integration challenges are common. The success of these digital investments hinges largely on user acceptance, particularly among doctors and nurses. Without a well-designed clinical portal, the potential benefits of interconnected systems are often unrealized, and digital initiatives may fail to deliver expected outcomes.

Mobile technologies, particularly tablets and specialized apps, are increasingly central to healthcare IT. While standalone apps have limited utility, they become highly valuable when integrated into broader digital ecosystems. They provide essential mobile access to clinical information, enabling healthcare teams to deliver coordinated, real-time care regardless of physical location. Mobile initiatives can vary from simple implementations to complex deployments, but when properly planned, they have the potential to transform how care is delivered.

Clinical analytics systems are becoming increasingly important, even if they are not yet a top priority for many organizations focused on data collection and accessibility. These systems convert raw data into meaningful insights, supporting population health monitoring, early trend detection, and financial performance analysis. As healthcare organizations mature in their digital capabilities, integrating clinical analytics should be a deliberate and scheduled component of any long-term technology strategy.

In summary, the foundation of successful healthcare digital transformation lies in strong data management at the infrastructural level. Once this is established, a wide range of advanced systems—such as care coordination tools, remote monitoring platforms, and diagnostic support systems—can be effectively implemented. Dr Saif Abed, a medical doctor, writer, and corporate strategist based in London, England, specializes in healthcare informatics and contributes regularly to nuviun. For more information about his work and his firm, visit www.abedgraham.com.

Animal rights activists engage in actions that may seem extreme—such as street protests, using bullhorns, distributing leaflets, chaining themselves to structures, organizing mass phone calls, filing lawsuits, publicizing animal research records, housing rescued animals, and even drenching themselves in fake blood—because they feel these measures are necessary to confront a global crisis. Billions of animals are subjected to abuse each year: discarded, beaten, electrocuted, tortured, skinned, and killed. Despite the availability of non-animal alternatives and bans on animal cruelty in some countries, the numbers remain unchanged. Those who perpetrate this abuse often operate with impunity, protected by laws that prioritize profit over ethics. Many are sociopaths who fear exposure, and when financial interests are involved, legal systems frequently shield them, even for the most brutal acts. The public often places blind trust in lawmakers and fails to question the reality behind animal suffering.

Animals used in entertainment are routinely beaten into compliance. Farm animals raised for fur endure unimaginable pain so humans can wear their skin. Activists argue that without visible, persistent efforts to expose these atrocities, the public will remain ignorant of the truth. They believe that if people could witness the cruelty behind closed doors—such as in taxpayer-funded animal research, circuses, and fur farms—they would be compelled to reject such practices. If these claims were false, abusers would welcome public scrutiny rather than labeling peaceful activists as “terrorists” to deflect attention. The more visibility activists generate, the greater the chance that society will confront the reality of ongoing animal suffering.

Therefore, individuals with influence—celebrities, public figures, the wealthy, and those with platforms—have a moral responsibility to use their status to amplify the voices of the voiceless. Simply posing for a campaign poster is insufficient. It is morally indefensible to possess resources and knowledge of animal suffering while doing nothing to stop it. High-profile figures like Meryl Streep could not realistically be silenced or punished for advocating animal rights, as their fame and wealth protect them from the legal harassment and public vilification that often target grassroots activists. If celebrities consistently participated in peaceful protests or championed legislation to end animal abuse, they could significantly counterbalance the financial and political power of industries profiting from animal exploitation.

A notable example is 73-year-old Oscar nominee James Cromwell, who was arrested on February 7, 2013, during a protest at a University of Wisconsin System Board of Regents meeting. Known for his role in Babe, Cromwell held up a large poster depicting a cat with a metal clamp implanted in its head and shouted about the university’s experiments on cats. PETA and Cromwell condemned the research, which aimed to help the deaf, as both cruel and ineffective. Cromwell stated in a video that up to 30 cats annually at UW had holes drilled into their skulls, were deafened with toxic chemicals, starved for days, and ultimately decapitated. He called the practice torture and criminal. After being taken into custody and later released, Cromwell joined forces with PETA spokesman Jeremy Beckham, who was also arrested. They were escorted out of the meeting in handcuffs.

In response, the director of the UW–Madison Research Animal Resources Center dismissed the protest as an attempt by outside activists to gain attention. He claimed that the USDA, the federal agency overseeing animal research, had conducted an exhaustive investigation and found PETA’s allegations baseless. However, images from the lab show a cat named Double Trouble, awake and suffering, in a facility that the USDA deems compliant with regulations. Cromwell later issued a statement explaining that after seeing distressing photos of Double Trouble and other cats subjected to invasive procedures, he felt compelled to join PETA’s campaign. He emphasized that the experiments—drilling holes in skulls, implanting metal coils in eyes, deafening animals with poisons, and starving them—are not only cruel but yield no meaningful benefits to human health.

The involvement of a celebrity like Cromwell has brought global attention to the issue, in contrast to the limited reach of grassroots efforts such as wearing animal costumes or distributing flyers. This highlights the power of public figures to shift public awareness and pressure institutions.

The University of Wisconsin–Madison has a long and troubling history of animal abuse. At one point, PETA ranked it as the worst animal research facility in the United States. This reputation is not surprising given the decades of taxpayer and student funding that have supported animal testing. The university has been linked to numerous documented abuses. Starting in the 1950s, Harry Harlow conducted psychological experiments on primates using extreme methods: monkeys were impregnated via rape racks, then their infants were separated immediately after birth and isolated for weeks, causing severe trauma. Researchers would then return the mothers to their offspring, observing violent reactions.

In the 1970s, Harlow continued his work by placing infant monkeys in small vertical chambers—known as “pits of despair”—where they were isolated for extended periods until they became motionless, hunched, and psychologically broken. Most did not recover and died in a state of permanent psychosis.

In 2004, three marmoset monkeys were killed when they were left in a cage during a sanitizing cycle. The cage was washed with hot chemical sprays, scalding the animals to death. Joseph Kemnitz, the center’s director, called it a “terrible accident” and suggested the deaths were likely quick due to heat exposure.

In 2005, the university faced criticism for testing Taser stun guns on pigs. Despite public outcry, Eric Sandgren, director of the Research Animal Resources Center, allowed the tests to proceed. The results showed no useful data applicable to humans.

In 2008, USDA inspections uncovered further violations. Primates were subjected to the “push-pull” method, where drugs were injected directly into their brains while they were restrained in chairs for hours or even days. One animal died during a lunch break taken by the researchers. These cases represent only a fraction of the documented abuses, with most experimental details remaining undisclosed.

Salvia canescens var. daghestanica, also referred to as Salvia daghestanica, is a compact member of the Salvia genus known for its exceptional tolerance to cold and drought. Native to Daghestan, a region in the North Caucasus of southwestern Russia, this variety is adapted to harsh northern climates and can withstand temperatures as low as -20 F (-29 C). It typically grows to just a few inches in height when not in bloom, reaching up to 12 inches (30 cm) when flowering. The leaves are approximately 2 inches (5 cm) long, featuring blunt serrations along the margins and a dense covering of silvery-white, woolly hairs on both sides. Over time, individual clumps can spread to a diameter of up to 2 feet (60 cm). Flower color varies from blue to violet or purple. While some sources indicate a flowering period from late spring to early summer, in practice this plant blooms from late April or May through late July or August, offering an extended display. Due to its small stature, resilience to extreme conditions, and attractive foliage, Salvia canescens var. daghestanica is well-suited for rock gardens and other low-maintenance landscapes. It dies back completely during winter and resumes growth early in the year, often emerging as soon as temperatures rise in March.

Ligated DNA was amplified via 16 to 18 cycles of PCR using primers specific to adaptor sequences and Phusion 2x premix (Finnzymes, Waltham, MA, USA). Following amplification, DNA was purified using QIAquick PCR Purification columns (Qiagen). Purified DNA was then captured on an Illumina flow cell for cluster generation and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq platform to produce paired-end 75 bp reads. For ChIP-Seq, six samples were multiplexed. Paired-end reads were demultiplexed and aligned to the mouse genome (NCBIm37) using BWA version 0.5.9-r16. Only uniquely aligned reads were retained for downstream analysis, and duplicate reads were removed specifically for H3K9,K14ac ChIP-Seq samples due to higher duplication rates; duplication levels were minimal in H3K4me3 samples. For H3K4me3, sequencing data from two biological replicates were combined into a single file. In RNA-Seq, eight samples were multiplexed. Paired-end reads were mapped to the mouse genome (NCBIm37) using STAR version 2.20c_r200 to enable spliced alignments. Biological replicates (two per condition) were maintained separately for differential expression analysis but merged to produce average expression profiles.

For RNA expression analysis, a GTF file containing ENSEMBL mouse transcript annotations (release 67) was used with HTSeq-count to generate a count table. Parameters included --stranded yes -mode union -type exon, which aggregates unambiguous read counts on the sense strand across all exons within each gene unit. Differentially expressed genes in wild-type ES cells following doxorubicin treatment were identified using the Bioconductor package DESeq. Genes were considered differentially expressed if they had an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and a fold change of at least 2.5. Genes with a base mean count less than 200—determined empirically—were excluded as they represent lowly expressed genes in both conditions. A differential expression heatmap (Figure 2A) was generated using Java Treeview. A normalized count table was used to compute expression values (Figure S2G in Additional file 3) and to identify the 2,500 most active genes in mouse ES cells by correcting raw read counts for gene length. Average profile plots for sense and antisense transcription (Figure 5C–F) were generated using normalized bigwig files for each strand, based on the direction of paired-end alignment, following the same method used for ChIP-Seq occupancy plots.

For ChIP-Seq occupancy analysis, all read depths were normalized to the total number of uniquely mapped reads per experiment. ChIP-Seq signal density was calculated as the average number of reads per base across 100 bp windows with a 20 bp sliding step. This was performed over a 6 kb region centered on the transcription start site (TSS) for promoter regions or over a 3 kb region centered on the peak summit for non-promoter regions. Custom Perl and R scripts interfaced with the Galaxy server were used for these calculations and are available upon request. Average profiles were created by plotting the median read density in each window across samples. For heatmaps, the sliding window data from wild-type ES cells were subjected to k-means clustering using Cluster 3.0. The resulting cluster order was applied to align the sliding window files from all other samples. Clustered heatmaps were then generated using Java Treeview.

RNA was extracted from cells lysed in TRI reagent (Sigma). After chloroform phase separation, RNA was precipitated with isopropanol and treated with DNase (DNA-free, Ambion). Total RNA (2 μg) was used for reverse transcription. RNA was denatured with 2 μg of random hexamers (Invitrogen Life Technologies Ltd, Paisley, UK) at 75°C for 5 minutes, followed by reverse transcription in a 40 μl reaction volume using 200 U of SuperScript II (Invitrogen) at 42°C overnight, followed by heat inactivation at 70°C for 15 minutes. The resulting cDNA was diluted in 300 μl of water and stored at −20°C until use.

For absolute quantification, 5×10⁵ cells were lysed in 1 mL of TRI reagent (Sigma), and 1 μL of a 1:20 dilution of ERCC Spike-in Mix#1 (Life Technologies Ltd, Paisley, UK) was added to each sample. After RNA extraction and reverse transcription, cDNAs were analyzed by RT-qPCR. Transcript abundances were normalized to the ERCC-00074 spike-in standard, with ERCC-00096 and ERCC-00130 used as secondary controls.

Protein extraction was performed by lysing cells in RIPA buffer (25 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate) supplemented with protease inhibitors. Lysates were sonicated using a Bioruptor (Diagenode) for 10 cycles (30 seconds each). Whole cell lysates were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes. All antibodies used are listed in Additional file 14. Oligonucleotides used for ChIP-qPCR, RT-qPCR, and splicing analysis are detailed in Additional file 15.

High-throughput sequencing data, including ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq datasets, have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession number GSE53492.

The provided text includes a list of scholarly references related to pediatric blood pressure measurement, normative standards, and predictive models for adult hypertension. Key studies include the Bogalusa Heart Study, which examines the predictive value of childhood diastolic blood pressure (K4 and K5 Korotkoff phases) for adult blood pressure. Other research investigates how the selection of diastolic Korotkoff phase in children affects the accuracy of adult hypertension prediction. Methodological considerations in determining blood pressure percentiles among normal-weight children are discussed, with attention to statistical approaches and data interpretation. Normative blood pressure references are presented for nonoverweight German and Korean children and adolescents, incorporating age, height, and sex. The European Society of Hypertension provides comprehensive guidelines for managing high blood pressure in children and adolescents. Comparative analyses of blood pressure levels across age groups in Chinese children, matched by height, are included, as are tools for identifying children requiring further blood pressure evaluation, such as simple tables and screening formulas. The study described in the final section, published in BMC Pediatrics, presents blood pressure tables for Chinese adolescents and justifies the inclusion of height, age, and sex as critical factors in establishing normative values. All authors contributed to the study's conception, data analysis, manuscript preparation, and critical revision, and they confirm no competing interests. The reflective technology originally developed for road safety in the UK—commonly known as "cat's eyes"—is now being applied to help protect whales. These road markers consist of glass spheres set in metal housings, used to delineate the center of roads. Popular from the 1950s through the 1970s, they were invented by a Yorkshireman who became a millionaire but maintained a modest lifestyle, with the only notable exception being his collection of televisions—likely acquired during the rise of color TV. His inspiration came from observing how a cat's eyes reflect light in the dark, a phenomenon rooted in feline anatomy that is explained in detail elsewhere.

Recent scientific advancements have led to the development of an underwater device that reflects tuned signals, including sonar. Since whales and dolphins naturally emit sonar pulses, this device can bounce a signal back when placed on underwater hazards like fishing nets. This reflection alerts whales to the presence of the obstruction, allowing them to avoid collisions. The device is particularly valuable for oil and cable companies needing to mark underwater infrastructure. Its key advantage is that it is passive—requiring no batteries or power source—making it durable and low-maintenance in marine environments.

It is a meaningful application of a simple yet effective principle derived from a cat’s eyes, now serving to protect endangered marine life. The refined sensory capabilities of cats, especially their acute vision and natural behavior, offer valuable insights. Their patience and innate grace serve as a quiet reminder of the wisdom found in nature.

A photograph by Stigs captures a striking detail: the reflection of a shiny floor within a cat’s eye, a rare visual observation. This image underscores the reflective quality that inspired the original technology.

The original article also briefly mentions unrelated content, such as a rescue cat named Logan, a ferret with dark ear wax, and a discussion on three types of feline mange, as well as a photograph of anatomical models of cats from La Specola in Florence, Italy. However, these segments are not directly connected to the central theme of cat’s eyes aiding whales.

In ancient India, the High Priest Ahmed Bey passed away and was cremated. His ashes were placed in a silver casket and transported to a remote mountain sanctuary, where they were buried alongside the family's sacred idol, which featured a prominent ruby in its eye. Following the burial, the tribe sealed the tomb and issued a curse against anyone who would disturb the resting place of their revered leader.

Centuries later, when Dr. Forbes brought the sacred Indian ruby back to the United States, the Whirling Dervish—a cunning and mischievous criminal—followed him home and assassinated him. However, the murder was not motivated by the curse, but by the thief’s greed for wealth and power.

Firefly investigated the crime and pursued the Whirling Dervish, who vanished into a whirlpool after leaping into a nearby river. Dr. Forbes’ daughter, still in possession of the ruby, traveled to Bombay to return it to its rightful resting place. Upon her arrival, the Whirling Dervish captured her and stole the gem. Firefly once again intervened, but this time the villain unleashed a fierce tiger on the two captives. The two managed to dodge the beast’s lunge, while the Whirling Dervish, caught in the chaos, fell from the stairs along with the tiger, both clawing at each other in the fall.

The fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet system in Europe marked a transformative moment, raising the central question: what should be Europe’s primary concern in the aftermath of this great revolution? Key insights from Robert Schuman’s speeches are explored in the study New Cold War or Common European Home? The question of the millennium by D Heilbron Price. The phrase “Common European Home” was first used by Schuman in the 1950s and later revived by Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s to reflect the historic opportunity for European unity brought by Perestroika. In contrast, the term “new Cold War” has been invoked by various Russian leaders, including Defence Minister Igor Rodionov at NATO in 1996, and in December 1999, Russian Defence Minister Marshall Igor Sergeyev declared that relations with NATO were entering a new phase of deterioration. The book Russia and the danger for the European Union offers a detailed examination of how Schuman’s vision could be applied after the revolutionary changes of 1989–91 and the consequences of current European policies.

In 1950, Robert Schuman declared that the European Community would be open to all European nations. When asked by a journalist whether Russia was European, Schuman replied affirmatively. This statement prompted American skepticism: was Schuman aiming to win the Cold War or to end it? Schuman responded that while he doubted the Kremlin would allow any of its satellite states to join under existing conditions, if such a move were ever permitted, it would be beneficial—promoting greater European unity and bringing more of Europe’s military potential under supranational control.

Schuman did not predict the exact timing of Soviet power’s collapse, but in January 1959, he told three young members of the European Parliament in Strasbourg that the fall of the communist system and its power structure before the end of the century was certain. He added that he might not live to see it, but the younger generation likely would, assuming a normal lifespan. At the time, the Soviet Union was at the height of its influence, with firm control over central and eastern Europe. The USSR’s launch of Sputnik in 1957 had not only initiated the space age but also instilled global fear that such technological prowess could be weaponized for global dominance.

The central question remains: was the creation of the European Union primarily motivated by the expectation of the Soviet Union’s collapse? Schuman’s vision was clear: Europe must be built not only for free peoples but also to welcome those from the East who had been liberated from repression. He emphasized that all those who wished to rejoin Europe in a reconstituted Community were integral parts of a living Europe. He paid tribute to their courage, faithfulness, suffering, and sacrifices.

Schuman’s warning to European political leaders was urgent: they must be prepared to receive these countries into the Community, as this would be their best guarantee for peace. Yet more than a decade after the Berlin Wall fell, many of these nations remain excluded. Instead of readiness on the part of Europe, the burden has been placed on the poorest and least capable countries to meet an overwhelming requirement—implementing 80,000 pages of EU legislation. A new barrier, not of concrete but of paperwork, has emerged in place of the old wall. Is unity truly conditional on the tomato farmer in central Europe using the correct pesticide? This standard raises serious ethical concerns in light of the 60 million war dead, the wounded, victims of concentration camps and gulags, and the countless lives shattered in pursuit of a freer, fairer, and more just Europe. For Schuman, political action was rooted in a clear-eyed assessment of realities, possibilities, and responsibilities.

Schuman also warned against delaying European unity by imposing excessive prerequisites. He stated that European integration could no longer wait, or it would come too late to save Europe by itself and for itself. By multiplying conditions, unity becomes unattainable. He rejected the idea that incompleteness justifies postponement: lack of perfection is no excuse for inaction. Bold action, he argued, is preferable to resignation. The principle of supranationality must guide the process.

Today, the conditions for joining should be consistent with those of 1950: respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, and a genuine willingness to embrace a supranational system of governance and solidarity, adapted to contemporary challenges. The Czech President Vaclav Havel compared the events of 1989–91 to the fall of the Roman Empire, underscoring the magnitude of the current political challenge. Yet, ten years later, Europe is witnessing growing antagonism between its eastern and western parts, accompanied by organized crime, corruption, ethnic conflicts, and war. Schuman’s efforts led to the European Union as a stabilizing force in Europe’s turbulent history. However, many candidate countries are becoming disillusioned with the prospect of joining due to the lack of vision and bureaucratic rigidity among European leaders. Schuman identified this as the primary danger facing supranational institutions.

There are two distinct issues: achieving peaceful unity across Europe—our highest priority—and securing full EU membership. Supranational cooperation enables nations to tackle shared challenges collectively. The response must address the most pressing needs of people, allowing for the creation of a community based on key areas of common interest. The initial success of the European Coal and Steel Community demonstrated that integrating vital sectors could make war not only unthinkable but materially impossible. This treaty could be renewed as a pilot framework for future full members. The rule of law remains fragile in some countries—while legislation may be passed, enforcement is often lacking. Immediate application of these rules would be an act of mutual trust, demonstrating commitment from both sides. From there, new shared goals can be set, fostering new synergies across Europe in other sectors. These initiatives could save vast resources and generate employment, effectively creating a self-funding mechanism for integration.

The current policy, however, has proven problematic. Demanding that former Comecon countries achieve the same level of development as market economies with over fifty years of integration has delayed the healing of Europe by more than a decade. Some countries are increasingly struggling to meet these demands, and the gap between aspiration and reality continues to widen.

The HealthMap system detected a media report about cholera cases in Ethiopia. The Ethiopian Public Health Institute confirmed 525 cases and 16 deaths linked to cholera infection. These cases were reported across the Oromia, Amhara, and Tigray regions, as well as in Addis Ababa city. A request for information (RFI) was issued on 12 June 2019 at 10:31 AM EST.

A response to the RFI was received on 3 July 2019 at 9:43 AM, including a press release from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute dated the previous day. Updated figures indicated 871 confirmed cholera cases across five regional states—Oromia, Amhara, Afar, Somali, and Tigray—and two city administrations, Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa. The case distribution was as follows: 360 in Oromia, 202 in Amhara, 131 in Afar, 33 in Somali, 19 in Tigray, 125 in Addis Ababa, and 1 in Dire Dawa. Seventeen deaths were reported, with 14 of those occurring in the Amhara regional state. Laboratory testing confirmed that 32 of the cases were caused by Vibrio cholerae. The outbreak was officially verified by the EpiCore system.

Mamma Andersson’s fifth exhibition at Stephen Friedman Gallery centers on a new body of work comprising unique woodcut prints, marking her first solo show dedicated exclusively to this medium and representing a significant evolution in her artistic practice. These prints portray enigmatic figures and scenes described as “characters who will not be pinned down: fleet of foot, they move swiftly across centuries, indifferent to mortality and geography” (Jennifer Higgie, 2017). Known for her evocative paintings that evoke a near-hypnotic sense of familiarity while omitting modern life, Andersson here extends her distinctive visual language into printmaking. Alongside the prints, three large-scale paintings on canvas deepen the narrative, exploring the same themes and mysteries. This marks the first time Andersson has translated her aesthetic into woodcut, with each piece hand-printed with meticulous care onto fine Japanese paper. Each print is singular, shaped by the unpredictable qualities of the woodblock’s texture, the ink’s viscosity, and the precise placement during printing—factors that ensure no two impressions can be identical. Rejecting printmaking’s traditional goal of reproducibility, Andersson embraces the inherent unpredictability of hand printing, incorporating subtle shifts, misalignments, and imperfections as integral to the work. As a result, the series forms a cohesive group, yet each print conveys a distinct emotional tone through its thick, oily pigment.

The conceptual foundation for these prints emerged during Andersson’s time at her summerhouse on Gotland, a rugged island off Sweden’s east coast. The arrival of an old printing press revitalized her studio space, infusing it with new creative energy. Motifs such as hares, red deer, black cats, and trees swaying in the wind reflect her roots as a landscape painter and her deep connection to the Swedish countryside. These images also nod to enduring cultural practices like hunting and fishing, underscoring Andersson’s preoccupation with the passage of time and the persistent, primal desires that define human experience.

Each of Andersson’s exhibitions unfolds as a narrative. In this presentation, a recurring image appears in varying hues, evoking a character at different moments across a day, each iteration carrying a different emotional or psychological nuance. When viewed collectively, the prints invite the viewer to construct a personal story. Individual vignettes, such as the cave and the headless statue, reference the 1957 discovery of Roman sculptures in a grotto at Sperlonga, Italy. These fragmented relics, with missing limbs and heads, carry an aura of mystery and childlike wonder. Andersson reimagines one figure by dressing him in 1970s-style shoes, a cape, and stockings, placing him in a new journey across time—an approach characteristic of her work: “Nothing is neat here. Nothing is clear. Nothing is stable – not even time” (Jennifer Higgie, 2017).

Gallery Two features three of Andersson’s largest paintings to date, executed on canvas rather than her customary wood panels. These works closely align with the prints in both style and technique. One painting conjures a fictional cave, evoking the atmosphere of a child’s imagination or a storybook. Another depicts a piano draped in delicate lace, a symbol of a fading art form—though we still hear its music, it is played less frequently. The third painting presents the red deer featured in the prints, rendered here with expressive, dynamic brushwork. 

Andersson’s focus remains on the ordinary: the homes people build, the objects they cherish, the relationships they form, and the stories they carry. These works serve as metaphors for life itself, infused with emotional intensity and renewed imaginative force. This new series of paintings and prints reaffirms Andersson’s exceptional ability to transform the everyday into images charged with enduring mystery and timeless resonance.

What are chemtrails, and how are they impacting our food and water supplies?  
Just when it seemed like Monsanto’s controversial activities were behind us, new revelations suggest they may be involved in something even more alarming—something that has been underway for decades.  
In the late 1960s, Monsanto reportedly backed the clandestine Muad’ Dib Geoengineering Lab, which was developing what became known as "chemtrail" technology. This initiative was framed as a humanitarian effort to combat global warming through weather manipulation. However, the supposed benevolence of this project is deeply misleading.  
Most people first learn about chemtrails through online sources, prompting them to look up at the sky and observe the extensive, grid-like patterns of white trails left by aircraft stretching across the horizon, eventually merging into a dense, hazy sky. These persistent trails resemble something out of science fiction. Initially, I assumed they were merely ordinary contrails—condensation trails formed by aircraft exhaust—but further research has led me to conclude otherwise.

Obesity is often met with judgment and stigma, reflected in common phrases like “You did this to yourself,” “Look at that person; he’s big as a house,” or “Can you spell exercise?” These attitudes reveal widespread misconceptions about obesity, which remains one of the most misunderstood health crises today. Misinformation about weight loss is constantly circulated by various so-called experts, promoting new fad diets and marketable diet products, while the reality is that over half of American adults are overweight, and about half of those meet the criteria for obesity.

Until the early 1980s, average body weights in the U.S. remained relatively unchanged, increasing by only a third of a pound between 1962 and 1980. The average adult male weighed 174 pounds, and the average woman weighed 145 pounds. However, societal changes—such as faster-paced lifestyles, larger portion sizes of cheaper, higher-fat foods, the rise of dual-income households leading to more restaurant dining and less home cooking, and suburban sprawl that reduced physical activity—contributed to a steady rise in obesity rates.

Obesity has since become a national public health emergency. According to the American Medical Association, nearly one-third of adults are now classified as obese. The CDC reports a 30% increase in obesity among adults aged 20 and older (defined as a BMI of 30 or higher), and a 16% rise among children and teens (defined by BMI-for-age at or above the 95th percentile on CDC Growth Charts). More than 60 million American adults and over 9 million young people are considered overweight. The CDC has set a goal to reduce adult obesity to below 15% by 2010, but current data suggest the problem is worsening.

Obesity disproportionately affects women (33%) compared to men (28%), with non-Hispanic Black women (49%) showing higher rates than Mexican-American women (38%) and non-Hispanic White women (31%). Men’s obesity rates remain consistent across racial and ethnic groups. Among teens aged 12–19, non-Hispanic Black adolescents have a 21% obesity rate, Mexican-American teens 23%, and non-Hispanic White teens 14%. The most alarming trend is the increasing prevalence among children: 22% of Mexican-American children, 20% of non-Hispanic Black children, and 14% of non-Hispanic White children aged 6–11 are obese, with an additional 15% of children and teens aged 6–19 at risk, falling between the 85th and 95th percentiles for BMI-for-age. In California, the situation is especially severe—overweight prevalence rose from 38% in 1984 to 57% in 2003, with increases across all demographic groups, particularly among those living below the poverty line.

Obesity is a serious health concern beyond societal perceptions of appearance. It is linked to stigma, discrimination, and social isolation. More importantly, it significantly increases the risk of numerous health conditions, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke, gallbladder disease, osteoarthritis, sleep apnea, respiratory issues, and certain cancers such as endometrial, breast, and colon cancer. In California alone, poor diet and physical inactivity are the second leading causes of death and disability, contributing to nearly 30,000 deaths annually. Eating disorders, which can be life-threatening, also intersect with obesity concerns.

Despite the complexity of obesity, many solutions are oversimplified, often reducing it to “eat less, move more.” This approach ignores biological and hormonal factors that influence weight, especially as people age. Physiological changes such as hormonal shifts and altered nutrient metabolism naturally promote weight gain over time. There is no single cause of obesity; rather, it results from a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental influences, and behavioral patterns. While overeating and physical inactivity are key contributors, other factors play significant roles. Hormonal imbalances—such as low testosterone, excess estrogen, or declining progesterone and estrogen levels in aging women—can lead to abdominal fat accumulation. Decreased DHEA levels with age also impair metabolic rate. These changes can contribute to insulin resistance, commonly referred to as metabolic syndrome or Syndrome X, which is strongly associated with obesity. Emotional eating is another major factor, potentially responsible for up to 75% of overeating episodes.

Although Americans are consuming more calories than ever, they are also engaging in less physical activity. Dr. Marion Nestle of NYU highlights how the proliferation of fast food outlets, oversized restaurant portions, the decline of school physical education, and extensive screen time—on the internet, television, and other devices—fuel the epidemic. Dr. Michael F. Jacobson of the Center for Science in the Public Interest emphasizes that obesity is not simply a personal failing but a consequence of a car-dependent, sedentary lifestyle. He argues that lasting change requires systemic shifts in public policy and infrastructure, not just individual blame. The California Obesity Prevention Initiative underscores that the global spread of obesity stems from powerful societal forces that promote high-calorie, low-nutrient foods and discourage physical activity. These trends benefit food and beverage industries that profit from large, convenient, and heavily marketed food products.

Technological advances have reduced physical activity across multiple domains—workplaces, transportation, daily routines, and leisure. A renewed focus on academic performance, combined with budget cuts in education and heightened safety concerns, has diminished opportunities for physical play and structured physical education. Long work hours and the demands of single-parent households further limit time for exercise. Poor urban planning, suburban sprawl, and unsafe neighborhoods discourage walking, biking, and outdoor recreation. Excessive screen time remains a significant contributor to obesity in adults, adolescents, and children.

Early life factors also influence later obesity risk. High birth weight due to maternal diabetes, low birth weight, and lack of breastfeeding are associated with increased obesity risk in later life. Children who are breastfed at any point are 15% to 25% less likely to become overweight, and those breastfed for six months or longer have a 20% to 40% reduced risk.

While Benjamin Franklin was in London, Miss Read remained in Philadelphia and managed her household with diligence and prudence, maintaining a steady presence in Franklin’s life and supporting his ambitions from afar. Franklin recognized that his position at Keimer’s printing shop offered no real advancement or prospects for growth, as the work was unchallenging and the business lacked innovation or expansion. Despite this dead-end situation, he actively cultivated his skills, sought out new knowledge, and built relationships that would later support his entrepreneurial goals. George Webb, an Oxford-educated scholar, had fallen into indentured servitude in Philadelphia after being unable to repay debts incurred during his studies, illustrating how even educated individuals could face hardship in colonial America. Franklin’s inventiveness became a key asset in his rise; he devised practical improvements to his printing equipment and processes, such as a more efficient press setup, which enhanced productivity and quality. His big break came when James Ralph, a prominent writer and printer, took notice of Franklin’s abilities and encouraged him to pursue his own business venture. During his time working temporarily with Keimer, Franklin used the opportunity to establish his own network of contacts, including influential figures in Philadelphia, by offering reliable service and demonstrating initiative. He adapted his deist beliefs by focusing on a moral code grounded in reason and virtue, which he found not only personally fulfilling but also economically advantageous—strict moral behavior, he observed, enhanced trust and credibility in business dealings. Franklin was 22 years old when he launched his own printing business in 1728. Through the Friday night meetings of the Junto Club, he and his fellow members developed critical skills in debate, problem-solving, and collaborative planning. The club served their business interests by fostering mutual support, sharing resources, and creating a network of trusted associates. In his first year in business, Franklin maintained a grueling work schedule, often rising before dawn and working late into the night, which earned him a reputation for diligence and reliability, thereby strengthening his creditworthiness among local merchants and institutions. The Pennsylvania Gazette distinguished itself from competitors through its clean, professional layout and its diverse content, including news, essays, advertisements, and commentary on civic matters, making it both informative and engaging. Franklin used his position as publisher to build relationships with powerful politicians, offering them favorable coverage and access to public opinion, which helped him gain influence and support. When his primary business partner withdrew, it was his friend and fellow Junto member, William Hunter, who stepped in to save the business by taking over financial responsibilities. Franklin leveraged his connections within the Junto Club, his influence as a publisher, and his established relationships in the Pennsylvania government to secure the lucrative contract to print colonial currency, a move that significantly increased his wealth. He emphasized that the outward appearance of industry and frugality was just as important as the actual practice, because public perception shaped trust and opportunity in business and social life. Franklin systematically undercut his competitors by producing higher-quality work at lower prices, offering faster turnaround times, and maintaining a more professional image, which gradually drove them out of the market. He decided not to marry his first fiancée, Deborah Read, because he believed he was not yet financially stable enough to support a family. When he eventually chose to marry Miss Read, he risked social and financial backlash, as their union was delayed for years and faced disapproval due to the circumstances of their separation and the potential stigma of an unmarried couple living together. The first public library in America emerged from Franklin’s vision and the collective efforts of the Junto Club members, who pooled their resources to create a subscription library where members could borrow books, promoting education and intellectual exchange among the public.

A November 2012 study titled “The Impact of Running out of Money in Retirement,” conducted jointly by the Society, the Urban Institute, and the Women’s Institute for a Secure Retirement, reveals that working just one additional year past the age at which an individual becomes eligible for an annuity can boost the annual payout by an average of 9 percent. The research was commissioned to examine the causes of retirement savings depletion, identify the underlying risk factors, measure the extent of these risks, and highlight emerging trends for future study. The findings indicate that the benefit of delaying annuity receipt varies by income level: for the lowest income earners, the increase can reach up to 16 percent, while for the highest income earners, it can reach up to 7 percent. Extending work by five years beyond eligibility leads to an even more substantial increase—up to 98 percent for the lowest income group—compared to gains between 42 percent and 71 percent for individuals in higher lifetime earnings quintiles. The report also underscores the advantages of delaying retirement for Social Security benefits. Using a hypothetical couple both aged 60—where one earns $100,000 annually and the other $50,000—the study shows that retiring at age 62 results in cumulative Social Security payments of $1.65 million by age 80. If the lower earner retires at 62 and the higher earner delays until 70, the total rises to $2.373 million. If both delay retirement to age 70, cumulative payments reach $2.425 million. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the significance of preparing for unexpected life events, or “shocks,” noting that 67 percent of men and 70 percent of women will face at least one such shock within a nine-year span. These shocks include medical conditions—experienced by 67 percent of married couples and 50 percent of singles over age 70—severe disability (29 percent for both men and women), cognitive impairment (19 percent and 17 percent respectively), and nursing home admission (23 percent and 22 percent respectively).

Pat Farrell asked if a certain behavior is documented somewhere. The response explains that it's part of the JavaBean conventions, not exclusive to Expression Language (EL). While EL is often associated with web frameworks, its roots lie in these broader JavaBean standards. The speaker expresses frustration with EL documentation, noting that although EL has its own specification and is well-documented in theory, the actual specification document is poorly structured and difficult to navigate. This difficulty is partly due to Oracle’s push for JSF (JavaServer Faces), which causes the EL specification to conflate JSP-specific and JSF-specific features, creating unnecessary complexity. As an alternative, the speaker suggests consulting the JSP 2.0 Specification, which treated EL as a core part of JSP and focused solely on that context, making it clearer and more straightforward—though it lacks updates from later JSP versions like 2.1 and 2.2.

Pat Farrell further comments that experimenting with new EL constructs—such as conditional expressions or non-trivial loops—often takes a long time due to unclear syntax. The response clarifies that this confusion may stem from conflating EL with JSTL (JavaServer Pages Standard Tag Library). EL is purely the expression language used to access data, while JSTL provides a set of tags for control flow and iteration. The JSTL specification is actually considered well-written and accessible. The speaker acknowledges that many Java specifications are notoriously hard to understand, with the Servlet and JSTL specs being relatively clear, while the JSP spec is notably worse. Some other specs are so obscure or poorly written that they might as well be in a fictional language like Klingon.

Despite these frustrations, the speaker admits to being unusually tolerant of this complexity. Colleagues often find it baffling that they can work comfortably across multiple languages and frameworks, whereas most stick to a single language like Java or C. For the speaker, this diversity is a source of engagement and interest—writing only Java all day would be unbearable.

Home repossession is a serious financial threat that can result in the loss of your residence and long-term consequences for your credit and financial stability. Understanding the risks and taking proactive steps can help you protect your home and maintain control over your future. This guide outlines the potential impacts of repossession and provides actionable strategies to prevent it.

The consequences of home repossession go beyond simply losing your house. It often leads to emotional distress, as being displaced from a familiar environment disrupts personal stability and well-being. Financially, repossession severely damages your credit score, which can remain on your credit report for years and hinder your ability to secure loans, credit cards, or favorable interest rates. Additionally, landlords may be reluctant to rent to individuals with a repossession on their record, limiting housing options. Financially, the sale of a repossessed property typically yields less than market value, and any remaining debt—known as a deficiency—may still be your responsibility, leading to further financial strain.

To avoid these outcomes, consider the following strategies. First, maintain open and honest communication with your lender as soon as you anticipate difficulty making payments. Most lenders offer hardship programs and are willing to work with borrowers who reach out early. Explore options such as loan modification—adjusting terms like interest rate, repayment period, or payment structure—or refinancing to secure a lower rate and reduce monthly obligations. These changes can make your mortgage more manageable and help you stay current on payments.

Seeking professional financial counseling is another effective step. A qualified financial advisor or housing counselor can assess your budget, help prioritize debts, and assist in creating a realistic repayment plan. They may also act as intermediaries between you and your lender to negotiate favorable terms.

If your financial situation is critical and continuing payments is no longer feasible, voluntarily selling your home may be a practical alternative. This allows you to settle your mortgage debt and potentially retain some equity, avoiding the more damaging effects of a forced repossession. Working with a knowledgeable real estate agent can help streamline the selling process and maximize your outcome.

Additionally, investigate government or nonprofit programs that offer foreclosure prevention assistance. These may include temporary financial aid, counseling services, or mortgage relief initiatives. Availability varies by location, so research local resources and contact relevant agencies for support.

If legal proceedings have already begun, consult a housing attorney. They can review your case, identify any procedural errors or violations by the lender, and help you pursue alternatives such as a repayment plan, short sale, or loan modification. Legal representation can significantly strengthen your position and improve your chances of a favorable resolution.

In summary, while the prospect of home repossession is distressing, timely action can make a meaningful difference. By communicating with your lender, exploring loan adjustments, seeking financial guidance, considering a sale, and obtaining legal advice when needed, you can take control of your situation and work toward a sustainable solution. Early intervention and support are key to preserving your home and protecting your financial future.

Frequently asked questions clarify common concerns. Home repossession occurs when a homeowner fails to meet mortgage obligations, prompting the lender to legally reclaim the property. Warning signs include missed payments, formal notices from the lender, or broader financial strain. It is possible to halt repossession even after it has started, particularly through legal action, loan modifications, or negotiations. Repossession negatively affects your credit score for several years, limiting future borrowing opportunities. Government and community programs are often available to help homeowners avoid foreclosure, and selling your home voluntarily is a viable option to prevent repossession and potentially retain equity.

Aging is a natural and unavoidable part of life, bringing about physical, physiological, and cognitive changes over time. While these changes are common, they do not automatically lead to a decline in quality of life. With appropriate support and care, many older adults continue to lead active, fulfilling lives while preserving their independence and cognitive function.

As people age, they may encounter several challenges that affect their ability to manage everyday tasks. Mobility often declines due to weakened bones and muscles, making activities like walking, climbing stairs, or rising from chairs or beds more difficult. Personal care tasks such as bathing, grooming, dressing, brushing teeth, or applying lotion may also become challenging. Maintaining a clean and safe living environment can grow harder, especially when it comes to laundry, meal preparation, and cleaning, which can compromise independent living. Reduced mobility may also make driving unsafe, limiting access to essential errands, medical appointments, shopping, and social visits. Cognitive changes, including memory loss or diminished mental function, can interfere with remembering important dates, managing medications, or making sound decisions. Additionally, social isolation and loneliness are common concerns that can negatively impact both mental and physical well-being.

Home care services provide valuable support to help older adults overcome these challenges. One major benefit is the ability to receive care in the familiar surroundings of one’s own home or residential facility, which promotes comfort and reduces disruption to daily routines compared to institutional settings like hospitals or nursing homes. These services are highly customizable, allowing care plans to be adjusted according to individual needs, preferences, and evolving health conditions. By assisting with activities of daily living—such as bathing, dressing, meal preparation, and medication management—home care helps individuals maintain dignity, independence, and autonomy, thereby enhancing their overall quality of life.

Home care is also a cost-effective alternative to institutional care. It often reduces the need for hospitalizations and readmissions, which can be expensive for both individuals and the healthcare system. Family members can actively participate in the care process, strengthening their involvement and emotional connection while also gaining peace of mind. Furthermore, receiving care at home lowers the risk of exposure to infections commonly found in hospitals and long-term care facilities, which is especially important for individuals with weakened immune systems.

Perhaps one of the most meaningful benefits of home care is the ability to remain in a familiar environment surrounded by personal belongings and loved ones. This sense of continuity can significantly reduce stress and improve emotional well-being. Caregivers are trained to provide a range of services, from basic personal care and companionship to more complex medical needs such as wound care, monitoring chronic conditions, and managing medications. This tailored approach ensures that each individual receives precisely the level of support they require, promoting both safety and independence.
